THE OBBILAZ BOY. The bird has sung its evensong. And sought its little Inivisy bed; • The homeless orphan lone y stands, s. • He has no place to lay his head. The mothers call their children home. Their happy faces thou can'st see. Homeless art thou, oh who can tell What place to-night will shelter thee. Poor child, within thy bright blue eyes • The pearly teardrops glisten bright; Thy form is weary, sore thy feet, Thy wan cheeks are thniugh hunger white. No loving mother's fond caress, No father's watchful eye to guide, • No sister's helpful spirit near, No shielding brother by thy side. Alone in this wide world, though young, A homeless wanderer doom'd to be; Sometimes a kind word cheers thy heart, God bless the heart that feels for thee. Only when sleep thine eyelids closet Dost thou forget thy life of care, In happy dreams again at home Surrounded by the loved ones there. Again a happy, case-free child, Thou roamest o'er the fresh green fields With all thy little playmates Each golden hour fresh pleasure yields. But non the morning gilds the sky. Dispelling dreams 14 friends and home; Again the cold world thou must face, A homeless orphan, boy to roam. • • One wintry night when cold winds blew, And stars were shining in the sky, There came a spirit form in white And took to heaven the orphan boy. St. Helene. J. G. ricKEssoiLL. _ _

SPRINGTIME IN AVENHAIt PARE. • At last she comes, the lingering, laggard Spring, For whom impatient hearts have waited long; Again we wander flowering trees among. Whose tints and odours mingled memories bring Welcome once more the swalloe's flashing wing. And listen to the cuckoo's changeless song. If Spring, by her delay, hath done us wrong, To make amends she now around doth fling, At once, in rich profusion, all the charms That oftenest in successive beauty come : With dappled blossoms on th' old fruit-trees' arms Mingle laburnums', chesnuts', rowans' bloom; Azaleas scent the air, and fragrant swarms Of hawthorn flowers, arid the sweet lilac's plume. May, 1881. D.

AN UNBIDDEN GUEST. A bird one day, as birds will do, • When times are hard, came hopping through ' An open window in the mill, When all around the place was still. It saw, no doubt, the golden store Of grain that covered all the floor, But never thought, in point of law, It had no right to what it saw. For birds are children of the air, Dependent on the Father's care, Who made for them His sun to shine, And gives them food by law divine. And so it hopped about the floor, And dined, and came next day for mere, And every day; and on the tree It used to sit and sing to me. —Lattle Magazine.
• 3fIZPAH. " The Lord watch betweea me and thee when we are absent one from another."

A broad gold band engraven With word of Holy Writ— A ring, the bond and token Which love and prayer have lit. When absent from each other O'er mountain, vale, and sea, The Lord, who guarded Israel., weep watch 'tween me and thee. Through days of light and gladness. Through days of love and life, Through smiles and joy, and sunshine, Through days with beauty rife; When absent from each other. O'er mountain, vale, and sea, The Lord of love and gladness Beep watch 'tween me and thee. Through days of doubt and darkness, In fear and trembling breath; Through mists of sin and sorrow. In tears, and grief, and death, The Lord of life and glory, The King of earth and sea, The Lord, who guarded Israel, Keep watch 'tween me and thee.—Argosy.

Which can "smell a rat" the quickest—the man who ' knows the most, or the teal who has the most nose? .4. man ranch addicted to atioriug remarked to his bed- fellow in the morning, "that he had 'slept like a top." " A know 5,- 011 have," replied the other, tartly ; "like a humming np," "If I have over usa.i any unkind words, Hannah," said Mr. S niley to Mrs. Smiley, refiectively, "1 take them sU back." "Yes, I suppose you want to use them over again,' was the not very soothing reply. First Vagabond: "Sec here, John, how do you stand on the question of the revival of the indome tax ?"—Second Vagabond Well, Joe, if the Government will provide me wi:h the income, I won't mind their taxing it." A master was expliintng that the land of the world was not continuous. He asked a boy, "Now, Jack, could your father walk round the world ?" "No, sir," said the boy. " And why ?" " Because he is dead, sir." " Mamie says you can't come to see her any more," said a boy to his sister's admirer. "Why not ?" "Because you cmae to see her seven nights a week nOW, and how could you come any More r" Silence was the only answer. A girl heard hoe Lather criticised severely across a dinner- table. The careless critic paused for a moment to say, "I hope he is no relation of yours, Miss L.?" And, as quick as thought, she replied, with the utmost nonchalance, "Only a connection of my mother's by marriage." WaLHEIL—The surname Walker has nothing to do with pedestrian ideas, but had its origin in trade and occupation, like other familiar names, such as Smith, Farmer, Bowyer, Fisher, and so on. Walker is a Common surname in York- shire, as will be understood when we explain its connection with the industry of that region. It is of Flemish deriva- tion. A man who worked at the walke (walche) or fulling mill was a walker, and in early Manchester directories all the fullers and cloth dmsers were called walkers. —Leisure Hour. LETIME TO THE NlLE.—When, after the founding of Fustat, the Nile did not rise to its proper level, Rm./Vas relate; that the Copts implored the governor Ammo to allow them to offer a victim to the river. The general refused, but when the Nile remained at its low level and famine seemed to threaten the land, Amrao made the Khalif Omar acquainted with the state of affairs. His messenver came back with a letter and the order to cast it into the Nile. Amroo obeyed, and in the very next night the Nile reached the required level of sixteen ells ; the letter of the Cona- mander of the Faithful contained these words: "To the blessed Nile of Egypt. If up till this time thou bast flowed only by thine own will, then cease to flow; but if thy ;dream was obedient to the command of the most high God, we beseech that God that He will grant thee thy necessary is- crease." This pretty legend is hardly credible, because the ancient Egyptian faith torbid human sacrifice as strictly as the Christian religion itself. However, in pre-Islamite times some kind of offering was no doubt cast into the stream, though not a maiden.—Egypt: Descriptive, His- torical, and Picturesque. Roams AUT.—In painting and sculpture, as already noticed, there is hardly such a thing as real Roman work; for though every Roman house of the higher class was full of their products, the Romans themselves to the last despised the mere handicraft of art, and were content simply with buying and admiring. They were conn-;ssehrs, but not artists. As Virgil says, others might carve a, title into life, or give breath to bronze; their art it was to rule the nations with their sway, to spare the humble and war down the proud. Hence there is no distinctive Roman school as op. posed to the Greek school. The Roman province in the world of art was simply to diffuse the Greek in countries which it wmild not otherwise have reached. T. Greek sculpta:e 1 painting of the later age does indeed differ from that of the earlier time. It is less stately, less pure, less ideal, more cosmopolitan, and more given to mere tricks of art and pretty fancies; but it is not on that account . more Roman. It represents, in fact, the style of art which naturally grows up for the gratification of wealthy but not very highly refined patrons—a style of art in which mere passing pleasure rather than the highest artistic qualities are aimed at. It lacks severity, ideality, and grandeur; it fritters itself away for the most part on mere prettiness and fanciful ideas. These are the inevitable signs of a degenerate age.—Cassell's Popular Educator. THE CHILDREN IN THE WOOD.—Addison refers to this popular ballad as "one of the darling songs of the common people" and "the delight of most Englishmen in some part of their age." Ile also points on,, that the incident where the robin-redbreast covers the elt, dren with leaves had a parallel in Horace. The Rom to Vt tells ns that when a child he fell asleep in a desert wood, whereupon the turtle- doves took pity on him and covered him with !eaves. Old iterature supplies many instances of the supposition, gene- rally entertained, that the robin covers the bodies of the friendless dead with leaves. Shakspere, Drayton Webster, Dekker, and others furnish examples of this. Authorities differ as to the origin and date of the ballad. Percy believes it to have been suggested by an old play entitled "Two Lamentable Tragedies the one of the murder of Maister Beech, a chandler in Thames Streete, Szc. The other of a young child =lnhered in a wood, by two ruffins, with the consent of his unkle. By Rob. Yarrington." (1601. 4t0.) Sharon Turner, in his " History of England," says :—" I have sometimes fancied that the popular ballad may have been written at this time the period of Richard lII.] on Richard and hisnephews, before it was quite safe to stigma- t'se him more openly." This theory, however, that ttichard was the wicked uncle referred to, does not find much favour. 'ayland Wood, near Walton, in Norfolk. and the village if Wood Dalling, alike claim the distinction of being the plac, where the tragedy was enacted, but tradition generall, accepted assigns it to the former place. The full title the ancient ballad in the Peyps collection is,. The Childrei is the Wood; or, the Norfolk Gentleman's Last Will Testament: arn to the tune of Rogero, &c."—Cassell's Illus. ried British Ballaels.

Perhaps I we do the great historian an injustice, for tie dwells with ' pleasure upon the extraordinary changes in the aspect of rural England since the days of the late Stuart king. We may, however, be allowed to glorify the turnip a little just at the time when farmers are devoting special atttention to its cultivation. What would England be without it? Think of it, if you can, ye townspeople. If, as we are informed, Lord Viscount Townshend, who represented England at the States General, introduced the turnip, he is worthy of a I higher monument than the Duke of York. We owe fresh meat for eight months out of the twelve to his enterprise. We owe our freedom from scuivy, leprosy, and other dis- agreeable consequences of feeding upon salt flesh, to him. 1 The wonderful increase in population in these countries I would not have been possible without the turnip. The em- ployment of millions LelL49 upon the turnip. The invest- ment of millions sterling is due to the turnip. The turnip is one of the main stays of England, and the Lord Chancel- lor might well sit upon one, instead of a woolsack, were it not a trifle too hard, and otherwise incommodious for such a purpose. Poets, statesmen, and historians, are apt, to con- sider the acts of kings and of Parliaments as of the first importance; but, to the vast majority of mankind, who , governs is of no matter whatever. Work and food are of more importance, and it is difficult to exaggerate the value of the turnip as a source of both.—Agrtcultural Gazette. ECONOMY IN MORWAY MANAGEsIENT.—Land is of 'opinion that the solution of the highway question lies in economy of management. It says :—There is a phenomenal highway board at Otley, in Yorkshire. So far as our ex- perience extends, it is the only highway board which has had anything to say for itself during the hubbub of the last three or four years as to the cost of highway management. We have more than once contended in these columns that, properly worked, our existing system of road management could be made not merely more satisfactory, but even cheaper, than the old parochial system. From Otley comes a striking confirmation of our contention. Mr. Francis Darwin writes a very interesting letter relative to the Otley highway district, which was founded in 1876, and contains 115 i miles of district and 28 miles of main roads. Under the parochial -system these roads had cost an average of £1,480 per annum; last year they cost £1,174; and this year they will probably not cost more than .£1,200. The condition of the roads has, moreover, been considerably im- proved, although they are not in the perfect state in which the board yet hopes to place them. The conclusion to which these figures lead is, Mr. Darwin thinks, "that if highway districts are formed containing not more than 150 miles of roads, a really efficient surveyor and clerk be ap- pointed, and a sincere desire be evinced by the highway hoard to work the system efficiently, the repairs of the road can be more effectually and with greater economy carried on by a board than by the parishes, besides removiog the inequity or parochial rating which once existed." A New BREED OF FINE WOOLLED SHEEP,—The WOOI of merino sheep, it appears, is just now very much more in demand than our coarse, stout, English long wools, which are only adapted for combing purposes; and some people think that the reason French manufacturers have such a great advantage over English ones in the classes of goods on which fashion has set its mark, is because the wools they have at command are BO very fine in staple. Just the kind of animal needed has been bred by Mr. Robert Russell, of Horton, Kent. This gentleman, when in Austria some years since, was much struck with the extraordinary good qualities of a superior flock of merinoes he saw there, and he brought some of the ewes home with him to cross with English long-wool rams as an experiment.' Lie has now created quite a new breed of such fixed uniformity of type that it deserves to be considered an original pure variety nearly as much as the Oxfordshire Down, Mr. Russell has quite a large flock at the present time, which has just the same feeding and treatment as his pure-bred Hampshire I Downs, and, whale of- equal grazing character, yield far heavier fleeces of a very valuable description. In fact their weight, taking ewes, tegs, rams, and all together, averages about 121bs. each, and the threads, although long, are at the same time of a beautitul silky character. If a plentiful supply of this sort of wool would enable the Brad- ford manufacturers to compete with their French rivals, all the Yorkshire flockmasters would have to do is to adopt Mr. Russell's new breed, and the knotty problem would be solved which has caused agitation of late. DARBY'S DIGGER. Darby's Digger for several years has been familiar to fre- quenters of the principal agricultural shows as an imposing and somewhat complex apparatus. The determination, enthusiasm, and practical tact of the inventor have enshled, him to overcome many difficulties and Secure the satisfac- tory working of his machine. At the Royal Agricultural Society's Carlisle meeting in July. 1880, it deservedly received a special medal as "a new implement for the cul- tivation of the soil by steam or other mechanical force." The Carlisle machine has satisfactorily dug 400 acres, and is still doing remunerative work.- Now, however, a stronger and rather more effectual implement has oeen turned out, which has been carefully tested during several days lately at Writtle, three miles from Chelmsford, and will be again at work this week at the Bath and West of England Show at Tunbridge Wells. The appearance' and construction of the new machine are little changed, It Consists of a loco- motive boiler' with a fire-box in the dehlre, tubes on each side, and a funnel at each end. The eight-horse power engine, fixed on the top of the boiler, has a single cylinder 9in, diameter, with 12in. stroke and 120 lb. pressure. The engine is suitable for thrashing or other farm work. On the crank shaft are two pinions, one driving the four travelling wheels which are 31- feet high with tires 2f 5. wide, the other driving the diggers, which are at the back of the apparatus, and consists of three sets of forks, each set containing 14 steel inch-square tines with chisel points, which keep them- selves well sharpened and are little liable to break. When the machine is to be moved through gateways, or has to propel itself along the road, the steering gear is removed and the wheels ace turned half round, when the width is reduced to eight feet. The steerage apparatus, formerly at the rear, now runs in front, preventing compression of the finished work. The regulation or the depth can be simply and promptly managed without stopping. Spiral metal springs on the shaft regulate each est of forks and give them the requisite amount of play. An extra spring in front of the pinion carrying each !set of forks would bene- ficially diminish jarring. Wrought iron has in many parts been substituted for steel, and in case of breaking is more easily replaced. Governors on the engine would instue more steady work. The digger has done good service for hire, the farmer at , Wrlttle paying 20s. an acre for digging the rye-grass stubble ' just eaten off by sheep. On these terms Mr. Darby pro- vides coal, of which one ton is consumed for the day's work of ten acres. The hirer draws water, of which aleaut 200 gallons, or 18ewt., are required every hour, which is drawn from the cart into the tank by an injector. A man atod boy , suffice to work the digger. The land at Writtle is a friable loara, dry, and in a favourable state for cultivation. The digger takes fully 20ft. at each stretch; the tines cut 10in. to llin. breadth; the depth can be regulated from 2in. to 12in. When we saw it about flin. depth was being done, but the depth varied a little when going up or down bill. The three great forks, 61ft. each, as the machine advances, are raised. in rhythmical order about 15i0. and thrown back about 2ft. In quick succession each fork inserts its 14 blades into the soil, and deftly turns the furrow slice. The three forks acting one after another power is economised; weight is also thrown off the wheels; the thrust of the forks besides helps the apparatus forward. 'I behest and most re- gular work was done when the machine was going' as it readily can do, at the rate of 100 feet in two and a quarter minutes. At a slower pace the slices were not as regularly cut or turned over. By a slight alteration of the machinery the land can be turned entirely over, as is often done in dig- ging, placed on edge as in ploughing, broken down fine, or lefe rough. An important feature of the work is the tearing out of twitch, thistle, docks, and other weeds, uncut, and thus more effectually insuring their destruction. Several Essex farmers who have had two season's' experience of the digger assure me that their land which has been dug has now fewer thistles than that worked by horses or steam plough. Proceeding across the ground already dug, the ap- paratus, although weighing 14 tons; is so well balanced on the four broad wheels that it does not seriously compress the loose soil, but turns it up in a very':Workmanlike man- ner. The calculated weight on the wheels per inch width of the tires is stated by the Royal Agricultural Society's en- gineer to be 3161 b. Ponderous although the' machine ap- pears, it turns readily, whether on the rye grass stubble or on the upturned ground, in little more than half a minute. Its capabilities lor cutting up hard well-firmed ground have recently been fairly tested by its successfully digging half a mile of a field road which bad been in constant use for two years. In stony ground the tines are stated to stand better than the shares either of horse or steam ploughs. When the land is thoroughly wet the digger would probably drag heavily, but in such circumstances cultivation by any known agencies is undesirable. Making ascents, even reaching one in 25, skids are placed in the wheel, and effectively secure a firm grip. The practical performances of the Digger now entitle it to take rank as one of the recognised implements of modern agriculture. It will, doubtless, still undergo simplification land improvement; it may even be reduced from its present I price of £1,000; with its power economically applied in a very direct way it constitutes a cheap and effectual mode of successfully preparing the soil for most crops; it appears capable of turning over ordinary loam soils Gin, deep at a cost of 7s. an acre, or neveral shillings less than it can he done by horses. It is likely to be more extensively used, not only in this country, bist on the Continent of Europe and in the great treeless, stoncless prairies of :America. MMELLAN LOB.

A newly-erected water tank, holding 40,000 gallons, burst at Chelmsford on Tuesday. No one was injured, but con- siderable damage was done to property. About mid-day on Monday, a young man named Heyes, 27 years of age, residing at Harclyqgate, one of a party of excursionists to Windermare, was drowned whilst bathing in the lake. . _
The French Commercial Treaty Commissioners met again on Tuesday at the Foreign Office, to consider the question of the cotton and woollen goods duties. Several deputations

attended. Dr. Danell, Roman Catholic Bishop of Southwark, died on Tuesday morning rather suddenly. He has been suffering from diabetes, but was quite able to go about, and last Sun- day was one of the visitors at Cardinal Manning's. The London Gazette announces that the dignity of Baronet is conferred upon Lieutenant-General Sir Donald M. Stewart, Commander-in-Chief in India, and Major- General Sir Frederick Roberts, and heirs male in both in-
stances. Arr M.P. FINED.—On Tuesday, at the Newcastle Police-

_ court, Mr. Burt, M.P., was fined 20s. and costs for not com- plying with a magistrate's order, and having his child vac- cinated. The member for Morpeth did not appear, but was represented by Mcs. Burt. Mr. FORSTER, in thanking the Glasgow Liberal Msocia- tion for a resolution expressing confidence in him, says it . . . . „

- encourages him to persevere, in spite of all difficulties, in the determination to remove real grievances in Ireland while doing his utmost to restore order. Lord George Hamilton writes as follows to a Welsh cor- respondent :. "I personally should wish to make religious teaching compulsory in all Board schools, but the opposition such a proposal would excite would so retard the cause of religious education that I hesitate to support it." The Bristel magistrates on Tuesday committed for trial a man named Benjamin Hill, for having procured from a messenger in the telegraph office the contents of telegrams. The messages had reference to the absconding and capture in Calcutta of a Bristol bankrupt named Sidney Bees, now in custody on a charge of forgery. An attempt was made early on Sunday morning to de- stroy or damage the police station at Loanhead, a mining village near Edinburgh. A quantity of gunpowder placed in a piece of iron pipe was exploded under the windows, but very little damage resulted. There had been some drunken disturbances in the village on the previous night, and several men had been arrested and lodged in the lock-

up. The coroner's enquiry into the matter of the explosion at the Whitfield Colliery, North Staffordshire, by which 24 lives were lost, was concluded on Tuesday. The evidence showed that when the tire which caused the explosion had got beyond the control of the men, the manager (Mr. Edward Thompson) ordered them to send the horses up. Before this work could be accomplished the explosion occurred. The jury regarded the manager's conduct as cul- pable negligence, and he was committed for trial for man- slaughter. Tuesday's Gazette contains the announcement that the Queen has been graciously pleased to appoint Major-General Sir Edward Bruce Hawley, K.C.M.G., C. 13., to her Majesty's Commissioners on the International Commission appointed to supervise the evacuation of the territories ceded by Turkey to Greece, and their occupation by the Greek authorities; and also to appoint Major John Charles Ardagh, C. 8., RE., to be her Majesty's Commissioner to take part in the delimitation of the new Turco-Greek frontier. ALLEGED ABSCONDING} OP A BANIERUPT.—A Central News telegram says:—On Tuesday morning, at the Bradford Bankruptcy Court, Richard Ernest Cooke, recently carrying on business as John Cooke and Son. Bradford, should have appeared to pass his public examination. Mr. Vint, stated that he had reason to believe that he had absconded, and the examination was adjourned sine die. Cooke's liabilities were £190,000, and his bankruptcy was brought about owing to a sudden fall in North British Railway stock two months ago. The 18th annual conference of the British Association of Gas Managers was opened at Birmingham on Tuesday, and was attended by upwards of 500 representatives from all parts of the Kingdom. The Mayor cf Birmingham (Aide?-' man Chamberlain), in welcoming the guests, mid the restric- tions placed by Parliament upon the dividends to be paid; to shareholders had to a certain extent removed the incen- tive to invention and improvement. The secretary reported that there were now 675 members of the association. The gold medal of the association was awarded to Mr. G. Barker for his papeeon the construction of gas holders, the first premium to Mr. Frank Livesey, the second to Mr. G. Steven- son, and the third to Mr. W. F. Hartley. EXTRAORDINARY PHENOMENA AT PENDLE HlLL.—Con- siderable commotion has been occasioned in Clitheroe and the surrounding district dering the past few days owing to the circulation of the intelligence that a huge quantity of, insects of peculiar construction had arrived in the neigh- bourhood, and had located themselves in the vicinity oZ Pendle- Hill. The phenomena was first observed about 'fortnight ago by persons passing along the mid over Pendlq Hill, leading here Sabden to Clitheroe. What appeared tel onlookers as caterpillars were noticed to be crawling along the road in large numbers, and each succeeding day they increased until the road was almost black with them, and It was impossible to place the foot on the ground withoat crushing several of them. Day by day they progressed in their mysterious journey, until at length they arrived at the Wellsprings beerhouse. Whether the reptiles scented the savoury flavour of the contents of the inn has not yet been discerned, but certain it is that they seemed determined to make a call. The inhabitants of the establishment, not being accustomed to receive this species of visitors, soon dis- covered what threatened to disturb the tranquility of the place, and immediately set about to make a speedy onslaught on the intruders. Brushes were the chief weapons brought into requisition, but so numerous were the attackers that it required the inmates to be constantly sweeping in order to keep the premises clear. The insects are exceedingly voracious, and they eat up every bit of grass in a very short time, leaving some places quite bare. This strange army— no one can surmise as to where they have come from—for- tunately appear to be diminishing in numbers, but they extend from Wiswell to Mearley, a distance of about three miles. A great many people visited the famous hill on Sunday last, to witness this strange phenomenon, and con- signments have been captured and brought to Clitheroe. a quantity being open for inspection at Mr. Cowgill's, stationer, Castle-street. The insects are of a peculiar kind in this dis- trict, being about an inch long, of a dark colour, and with light stripes on the whole length of the body. GOOD TEMPLAR LAWSLTIT.—LEES V. MALINS.—The hear- ing of this case was resumed at Westminster on Friday, before the learned arbitrator, Mr. Wills. Nearly the whole sitting was occupied with the cross-examination and re- examination of Mr. Smyth, of Liverpool, whose evidence 11 went to prove the various transactions which led to the withdrawal of the British delegates from the Supreme Court. He acted with Mr. Melina in America, but on his return to this country changed his mind about the separation. He attended a special session called by Colonel Hickman, after the defendant And his associates had, by the latter, been de- clared in contempt of the Right Worthy Grand Lodge. At that meeting the plaintiff (Dr. Lees) was elected Grand Worthy Chief Templar, but it was not a meeting of the Grand Lodge. Towards the close of the day's sitting an argument took place between the learned Arbitrator and the counsel en both sides as to the effect of the evidence so far. The Arbitrator said, that though the circumstances of the severance at Louisville might be very interesting, he ' thought they had little bearing on the case, which depended more on what was done in England, or resolved by the Grand Lodge of England, than on what occurred in America. The question in dispute was one of property, and the plaintiff (Dr. Lees) would need to prove that a trust in the property existed on the part of the defendant Malin, on whose behalf he held the trust; that those for whom he held it had properly dispossessed him of the trust; and that the plaintiff had by them been deputed to succeed the defendant, and hold the property. The case was again adjourned.—Thehearingwas resumed on Saturday morning. Evidence was given for the plaintiff by Mr. Samuel Capper, Manchester, who said he had been a member of the Order since 1869, and attended the R.W.G.L. seesions since 1872. Subordinate lodges were controlled by the R.W.G.L. until the formation of a Grand Lodge, received the password from the R.W.G.L. each quarter, which would admit mem- bers to any lodge in the world. The defendant's party issued a different password to the one from the R.W.G.L., the result being to split up trio Order. He was requested, in June. 1876, by Colonel Hickman, to represent the R.W.G.D. • informed Mr. Matins, and also wrote to him ob- jecting with regard to parts of the manifesto of the Grand Lodge on the negro question. He gave an account of the discussion of the question at the Newcastle Grand Lodge meeting, where the manifesto was adopted, threatening separation, but no information was given that negroes had for years been admitted to the R.W.G.L. Acting for the R.W.G. Templar, who appointed him under special power conferred by the R.W.G.L., got up a memorial to the G.L. executive, signed by a large number, asking them to call a special session of G.L., but they declined to do so, when the affairs of the Order became more and more complicated. Sent Mr. Matins a copy of circular from the R.W.G. Templar, declaring Mr. Malins and others in contempt. He then issued a call for a special session of the Grand Lodge, sending to all the lodges he could reach. A number of lodges sent representatives, separate lodges instead of dis- tricts being invited to elect. The meeting was held, the R.W.G. Templar made a statement, and required the ap- pointment of new officers, which was done, and the plaintiff (Lees) was elected Grand Worthy Chief Templar. The de- fendant returned to the R.W.G. Lodge certain goods be held as agent. —The 'case was further heard on Monday. The IRev. Stephen Todd stated that there were present at the [Manchester meeting representatives from 100 lodges out of I about 2,000 then in existence, and that a present Grand Lodge of England, having formed Provincial Grand Lodges, now had 1,300 members connected with it in only nine I counties. Mr. Hector Davidson, Leeds, and Mr. William Hoyle, Bury, were also examined. The latter was chair- loan of a four days' conference of representatives of tie two sections, held in London in 1876, which failed to effect a reconciliation, and left him under the impression that the separation at Louisville was not justified. Mr. Stephen W. Ritchard, shipowner, Liverpool, detailed the proceedings at the London and Newcastle Giend Lodge sessions, in tte. course of which, while approving of the efforts to obtain admission of the negro race, he objected to the internation ii body being approached with threats. He was not aware of any misrepresentations on the question by Mr. Matins, ard objected to the course pursted by the plaintiff's party ie splitting up into several Grand Lodges.—The further hem' tog of the case was then adjourned till October. T Pali Hartley's Damson is unequalled.—ADVT.

, ,Government majority --63 One of the journals of the time remarked, " Mr. Gladstone won his Magenta gallantly, and with extraordinary damage to the enemy. The battle has been renewed, and is raging while we write, but the opposition army is dispirited and charges languidly, and all seems tending towards a Minis- terial Solferino. Mr. Gladstone distinguished himself in his first engagement by a feat of arms of the most brilliant character, and none of his own Homeric heroes could have more terribly 'poured in thunder on the foe.' When Mr. Gladstone addresses himself In his best manner to his work, as he did upon the occasion in question, the House of Com- mons is justly proud of its Illustrious member. Sometimes, like Burke, "He goes on refining " And thinks of convincing while they think of dining but there was no such waste of thought on this occasion when he closed with his adversary like a man who meant mischief, and he did it. Mr. Disraeli knows best whether it was wise to get his forces so exceedingly well beaten at the beginning of the financial campaign, but that is his affair and Prince Rupert's." The Repeal of the Paper Duty, which formed a very im- portant part of Mr. Gladstone's financial plan, and which was intended to effect a further reduction in the cost of newspapers, was opposed by Mr. Miles. It was in the debate on the third reading of the bill for the Repeal of the Paper Duty that Mr. Gladstone, for once in his life, talked against time. It became apparent to the Government On that par- ticular occasion that they were in danger—that their feet- were more numerous than their friends and that a division would under such cthh circumstancese destructioniiibme:frasttoanl. AdTmoibueistbceoatitz —destruction of that Administration would be to every irt f would eulPd dividual member of it for a longer or shorter interval of time, perhaps for ever, loss of place—and loss of pla.le meant loss of influence, loss of rank, loss of salary, lo- of everything the politician strives to gain. No 'won- der that the gentlemen who generally sit in very u graceful postures on the Treasury Bench evinced thedeepe-t anxiety. But in such circumstances there is nothing li, A Fabian policy, and there is nothing more -desiral, than a long speech. The man who speaks longs speaks best. Happily, Mr. Gladstone was on legs and there is no man who has such a wonderf faculty of speaking as himself. Indeed it has been sa that he could address the House for a whole week, and o

the Friday evening take a new departure, beginning with the observation—" After these preliminary observations I will now proceed to deal with the subject matter of my financial plan." On the occasion to which we refer Mr. Gladstone exercised this remarkable faculty to the utmost. " He," says an eye witness, "started vigorously enough, dashed with impetuous brevity through the great part of the subject on which he might have advantageously in- sisted, but all of a sudden he began to wind round and round, over and over again came the same arguments in almost the same words, and for once the Chancellor of the Exchequer was not almost, but I should say, quite prosy. The cause was obvious. The Treasury Whipper-in was seen flitting about, in and out, backwards and forwards, to the Treasury Bench with an anxious aspect of countenance. Ever and anon white-waistcoated gentlemen, evidently dragged from the opera or evening parties, were silently filling the Ministerial benches. At last the Treasury I Whipper-in entered the House and sat down upon the Treasury Bench with an air of complete satisfaction. The thing was done, narrowly but effectually, and then the Chancellor of the Exchequer eat down also." In spite of Mr. Disraed's reply all ground of anxiety had been re- moved and the Ministry had a majority—not a large one, but a majority when they were on the verge of a defeat. The Budget was passed at last, and we can only add that no skill in the handling of figures less consummate, no rhetoric less persuasive than that possessed by Mr. Glad- stone, no confidence less robust than that entertained by the country in his sagacity as a financier could have carried a Budget so startling and so bold with success through the storm of opposition which it had to encounter. Well might a writer in the Daily News observe—" The audacious shrewdness of Lancashire married to the polished grace of Oxford is a felicitous union of the strength and culture of Liberal and Conservative England, and no party in the House, whatever may be its likings or antipathies, can sit under the spell of Mr. Gladstone's rounded and shining eloquence without the conviction that the man who can talk shop like a tenth muse is after all a true representative man of the Market of the World." 7, Limefield, Blackburn.

HER MAJESIY'S PRIME MINISTERS. THE RIGHT HON. W. E. GLADSTONE. THE BUDGET OF 1860. In 1859, the Government of which Lord Derby was the head and Benjamin Disraeli the brains, having appealed to the country, and finding itself in a hopeless minority at once resigned office, advising her Majesty to send for Lord Palmerston. His Lordship succeeded without any difficulty in executing the task assigned him by the Queen, and re- turned to Downing-street with Mr. Gladstone as his Chan- cellor of the Exchequer. • • The Budget of 1859 need not detain us long. It was a thoroughly simple and at the same time a thoroughly honest measure. The expected income for the year was £64,340,000, while the expenditure was £69,207,000. Mr. Gladstone did not attempt to make up this deficiency by a loan or by any of the expedients usually adopted by Chancellors of the Exchequer for putting off the evil day, but by an addition of 4d. in the pound to the tax on incomes above £lso—a penny stamp on bankers' cheques drawn across the counter, and by the diminution of the malt credits from eighteen to twelve weeks, thus adding to the accounts of the year this duty which otherwise would not have been available till the year following. The year closed with unmistakable signs of prosperity. The Customs, the Excise, the assessed taxes of the pot-office yielded a revenue which surpassed that of any previous year by £2,023,000. The imports and the exports were greatly in excess of any previous year. Trade and com- merce were flourishing in all their branches. Pauperism was much diminished. Employments were plentiful, and wages high. The rate of discount was low, and money abundant. This hopeful state of things was further im- proved by the knowledge that Mr. Cobden was engaged in negotiating a Treaty with France, which, based on Free Trade principles, was calculated to give an enormous im- pulse to the trade between England and France, and to unite them by bonds that would render a war between them almost impossible. .He to whom the country owed the greatest measure of commercial freedom, with all its bound- less cense ofences of prosperity and tranquillity, that was NEW ZEALAND AND ITS RESOURCES. ever wrought out of the moral force of reason and opinion, and who, having declined high office in the State, was Our silent newsbearer, the New Zealand Herald, awaits us seeking in foreign travel the restoration of his health, found every morning on the breakfast table, and our first glance time and energy to devote himself to the elucidation searches the first "cablegrams," to learn what is doing and of those commercial principles to the promotion of which his saying in Old England; how rebellion fares in the Trans.vaal and in that home of discontent across the Channel; life had been devoted, and won an entrance into the very stronghold of Protection and Prohibition—doing more in how the Tarco-Greek dispute drags its slow length along. and whether prosperity has again and permanently visited this single act to establish the basis of that system of uni- our native land. A statue has recently been found in a mound pal the Egyptian Government Railway line. It believed bibs, 4,568 years old; and if this is confirmed, it will probably be one of the oldest known statues in the world. This statue is about being removed to Cairo. The Trustees of the Burns Monument at Ayr have, the Scotch papers say, completed the purchase of the cottage and the four acres of land fened by the poet's father in the year 1756. The cottage, which will no lodger be used as a public-house, will in future be open to visitor for a small charge. The purchase money .for the whole property was

£4,000 - _ . Dinsrszeratrr FOR Rooats.—M. &Mott proposes (Comp*. rend.) to employ "chamber crystals" as a disinfectant. He places a solution of these crystals in sulphuric acid in .the room or other place to be disinfected; the atmospheric moisture slowly decomposes' the liquid with liberation of oxides of nitrogen, which destroy organic matter present in

the air. It is said that Mr. Joseph Thomson, the young African crplorer, who is now fulfilling a commission intrusted to him n by the Sultan of Zanzibar, thinks of taking a some- what novel course with his account of his adventures. In- stead of waiting, as is usually done, till he returns home to publish his narrative he will probably send it home by in- stalments, to be published in one or other Of our magazines.

M. Phipeon states in Les Mendes that he prepares a zinc white by precipitating a sulphate of zinc by means of a solution of sulphide of 'barium, which displays a new and interesting actinic phenomenon. The precipitate is con- densed by hydraulic pressure, and heated to redness in a furnace arranged so as to prevent much oxidation. It is then a salt of snowy whiteness, which, when it is exposed to sunlight, speedily acquires a brownish tint, becoming in about twenty minutes a slate colour. If placed in darkness for five or six hours, it recovers ita originat whiteness. The experiment may be repeated any number of times with the

same specimens. - Two young I3aptist missionaries have just accomplished a notable feat of exploration on the Congo. When Mr. Com- ber made his last and unsuccessful attempt to teach Stanley Pool from an Salvador by way of the Makuta towns, two of his comrades, Mr. Crudgington and Mr. Bentley, started for the same destination along the north bank of the Congo. As their journey was only of a preliminary nature, they were in light marching order, and had with them very few carriers and stores. After about three weeks' hard travelling, they arrived at Stanley Pool, which Mr. Comber had vainly endeavoured for some eighteen months to reach by the other route. Want of provisions, of course, prevented a lengthy sojourn; and, after examining both banks of the river and visiting IK. de Brazza's station they returned to Vivi, Mr. Stanley's station below the Veneta FAIN where they arrived early in March. DISCOVERY AT Demescus.—Two correspondents at Da- mascus send to the Atheneum accounts of a recent dis- covery. Workmen had to remove a gateway, built of stones of considerable size. "When removed, these stones bore evident traces of having been taken formerly from, more ancient buildings. The carvings found on them were of two distinct periods. On one side the carvings represented a huge shell, evidently cut after the Mahornetan conquest and occupation of this country, whereas the part walled in had traces of the Greek Roman embellishments of the best Antonine period, of the same character as found on the architrave of the beautiful gate still preserved, and seen from the roof of the Bazaar of the Goldsmiths. One of these stones, 6ft. 10in. in length, has an inscription under its moulding in one line, from which it is evident that the monument on which it was inscribed had been erected in honour of three men—namely, Titus, Aijon, and, Righam, who are stated to have been treasurers of the temple. It is much to be regretted that the beginning of the legend is wanting, which would, no doubt, have informed us whether this lintel belonged to the mausoleum of these three persons or whether it once adorned one of the gates of the famous temple now converted into the great mosque known by the name of Jamie el Ammavi. In its immediate neighbour- hood the stone under consideration was discovered. The end of the inscription terminates with a date, of which ETO, the year, is all that is left. The date itself is miss- ing." A NEW EXHILARATING SUBSTANCE.—Dr. Luton, of Rheims, calls attention in a French medical paper to the exhilarating properties of the tincture of ergot of rye when associated with phosphate of soda. The circumstances of the discovery were as follow :—A woman of 82, at the in- firmary of he maisan de retraite, in Rheims, was receiving tincture of ergot of rye for disease in the knee. Fearing an unfavourable turn, the doctor thought to strengthen the ac-1 tion of that medicament with phosphate of soda, and accord= ingly combined a little of the two substances in a quarter of a glass of sweetened water, The patient, about three- quarters of an hour after taking this, surprised the inmateri by bursting into loud laughter, without obvious reason, and this continued for more than an hoar, with brief intervals: The laughter seemed to be absociated with merry ideas, and to indicate a kind of intoxication. For some time after it died down the woman was in great spirits and good humour. Dr. Luton had not witnessed the scene, but the consequences to the patient being good, he administered the substafice again, and a third time, observing the sarne effect. The ex. periments were further repeated on seven or eight women and girls, with hke results. In the case of men, the action of the substance is less marked; it appears only in colour- ing the face, giddiness, and slight headache. The effects in question have probably a common origin (it is thought) with those from eating rye-bread when, in,. rainy years, the cereal Contains at mud as five per cent of ergot. A sort of intoxication is produced; which theeonsumers by no means - ENGLISH AND., SWISS WATCHES.—Our Geneva corre- spondent writes :--."The comments made on my letter on the Swiss watch trade (which you printed on April 13), as well in your columns as elsewhere, have attracted some at- tention in Switzerland and been the means of eliciting fur- ther details concerning the principles on which the horolo- gical prizes at the Melbourne Exhibition were awarded. In reference to a remark of one of your correspondents, that the judgments of exhibition juries are by no means infal- lible, it is pointed out that, though there may well be dif- ferences of opinion as to the relative excellente of finish and outside appearance of several watches, good going is a matter of fact; and that the watches seat for competition to Melbourne were tested in the observatory and their respective time-keeping qualities ascertained beyond a pos- sibility of doubt. The highest number of points, as I have already mentioned (500 out of. a possible 500) was obtained by a Swiss. watch; next comes an English watch by Kil- patrick, of London (495 points). To them succeed the fol- lowing :—A Swiss watch, 490 points; English (Bukney), 485; Swiss, 480; a German watch, 470; Swiss, 465; Eng- lish (Bultney),4Bo ; Swiss,4ss ; English, 450; Swiss, 445 ; English, 440; German, 435; American (Waltham), 430; English, 425; American (Waltham), 420 •' English, 415; German, 410; English, 405; English, 400. No Swiss watch entered for competition gained less than 445 marks; no English wateh fewer than 400. The greatest number obtained by an American watch was 430; and four Ameri- can watches were sent to the observatory which, because they gained fewer than 400 marks, were not classed. It will thus be seen that, albeit Swiss watches showed a de- cided superiority, their English competitors ran them very close, while American watches were almost out of the run- ning. If the system of official testing which obtains in Geneva were established in England it could hardly fail to have a beneficial effect on British watch-making. , Genevan horologists can send their watches to the observa- tory here to be thoroughly tested, and the results of the annual competition are awaited with eager interest. It is a sort of watch Derby, with the difference that the best watch invariably comes in first, which is not always the case with the best horse. At the Swiss competition, the watches sent in for .competition used only to be placed in the refrigerator and stove 24 hours respectively, but they are now kept five days in each respectively, and errors of compensation are compared as well with the extremes of temperature in these two receptacles (about Meg. to 30deg. centigrade) as with the temperature of the room (from - to 17deg.).—The Times. •

=,-- AN OCEAN WAlF.—Walking one morning last winter—a day or so after the terrible Tuesday—on the Parade at Hastings. I happened to notice a curiously shaped flint among the shingle just thrown up by the great storm. The waves had beaten riulkt over the sea-wall, and scattered wrack and pebbles along the whole roadway. I stooped down and picked up the odd-looking fragment; to my sur- prise, I found it was a palwolithic implement, a rudely chipped flint knife of the older-stone age, the relic of a race compared with whom even the builders of Wanadyke here were men of yesterday. This rude flake was fashioned by the naked black-fellows who hunted the rhinoceros and the mammoth in the English valleys, before ever the great ice age itself had spread its glaciers over the length and breadth of the land, a couple of hundred thousand years since. Its outer surface was dulled and whitened by age, as is always the case with these primeval flint weapons; but its edge was still sharp and keen, though crusted in places with hard film of mineral deposit, and also blunted here and there by use in cutting clubs and reindeer bones for its savage pos. sessor. But there was no traces of rolling as in water-worn pebbles; the knife was freshly disinterred. It was clear 1 that the storm had just unearthed it from beneath the sub- merged forest which belts all the coast from Beachy Head to Dungeness. For the forest is a post-glacial deposit; and it once formed part of this great connecting land, now buried beneath the Atlantic, the English Channel, and the German Ocean. The trees which compose it still stand as upright stumps, firmly bedded in a layer of tenacious clay; and strewn beneath them lie prostrate boles, in the very places where the wind threw them down some fifty sr sixty thou- sand years ago. In the public garden at Hastings, one of ' these huge balks, dug up on the 'St. Leonard's beach, has been fixed as a curiosity; and, though its outer layer is charred and.blackened by the water, the inner wood is still as sound and firm as on the day it fell. For we have to deal here with a time which is marvellously ancient indeed when measured by our ordinary human and historical chronology, but which is quite modern when judged by the vast timepiece of COSIIIiCA and geological cycles.—Cosnhill Magazine. --_. . --

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MonnAr. The House met at five o'clock .for the first time after. the Easter recess, when the Lord Chancellor took . his seat on the woolsack. MINISTER OF SCOTLAND.—Lord &ma raised the ques- tion of the expediency of there being a Minister in the Cabinet to represent Scotch affairs, and who at the same time complained that Scotch bills In Parliament at the pre- sent moment were greatly neglected.--Tbe Duke of ARGYLL acknowledged tho justness of the latter complaint, but mid the English people had quite as much right to complain that their interests were being neglected. With regard to the advisability of there being a Scotch Cabinet Miniqter, the noble Lord said no assurance could be given that the Minister. would be a Scotchman, and he did not think the Scotch people Would like to be governed by a Minister ignorant of their. customs, manners, and wants.—The sub- ject was afterivards discussed by the Earl of Rosebery and the Earl of Airlee, in response to whom Earl GRANVILLE replied that he was not able to give, on behalf of the Government, a final answer for several reasons, but the block in the House of Commons of pressing business WA9 such that it was now clearly the duty of the Government to consider how to remedy the state of things.

IRISH Asr.apts.—Mr. FORSTER replying to questions, said that the Government had no legal proof that the Land League is :affiliated J with the Ribbon conspiracy and the! Fenian conspiracy. He had net found during his visit to Leland that the landlords are to any great extent, making use of theli4powers so ae to force the Government to support them in the exercise of injustice; he was of the opinion that a considerable number of tenants evicted were able to pay their rent, whilst e:Large proportion of the remainder failed through their own' fault; finally, he stated, that the riots' in West Cork had arisen from a rumour, entirely untrue. that it was the intention of the Govern- ment to arrest a parish priest named Murphy. THE lensu LAND BILL.—At half-past five the Committee on the Irish Land Dill) WAS resumed, and a remarkable and hitherto unprecedented disposition towards expediating the 'business was di:Splayed': Mr. Biggar stood first on the !wiper ,With 'an amendment fain.ing. the question of the subdivision Uf holdings, Which bad,iffready been exhaustivelydiscilased. Mr Gladstone, referring to this fact, thought it would be a Aquae of time further to discuss the matter.i Whereupon an tmexpected, ally appeared in the person of Mr—Parnell, who appealed to: Mr Biggar, not to proceed With his amendment, observing that it -was not ' his desire to obstruct the Bill, whilst at, the same time he held the opinion that it would be ineffectual for the purpose for which it had been designed. Several other members-Captain Aylmer, Mr. Errington, and Mr. A. Balfour—did not persist in the amendments which they had placed on the paper. Mr. Sullivan, in a very few words, moved to omit Sub-secetion 3, but no debate was raised, and the amendment was withdrawn. Thus in a few minutes a whole page of amendments was cleared, the Committee halting befere an amendment, moved by Mr. Macnagliton, ' by which it was desired to provide for the purchase of the tenancy by the landlord in case the parties differed. On a ' division, this was rejected by 193 votes against 130. This was the smallest niajority of the night obtained for the Gov- ernment, the majority rising over 200 when Mr. LEA pro- posed to substitute "fair market price " for "the value" of the tenancy. Shortly after eleven o'clock Mr. CHAPLIN moved an amendment,which once more raised the old que.tion of the meaning of tenant-right. At a quarter-past twelve Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL moved to report progress, which, after some remarks from Mr. GLADSTONE, Mr. TOM COLLINS appealed to him to withdraw. Mr. W. FOWLER took the opportunity of asking what steps the Premier pro- posed to take to meet opposition of this kind; a sugges- tion of obstruction which Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE in- dignantly protested against. Mr. GLADSTONE, amid cheers from the Ministerialists, said the considerations put forward by Mr. Fowler were not a single day out of the thoughts of the Government, and whilst desirous of surely feeling their ground as they proceeded they would be prepared to make to the Rouse whatever propositions might appear necessary for carrying the bill this session. The motion to report progress being withdrawn, the committee divided on Mr. Chaplin's amendment, which was rejected by a large ma- jority. Progress was then reported, and the remaining orders wets disposed of. The House was counted out at a quarter- past two.

PEASANT DWELLINGS IN IRELAND. Lord WAVENEY I asked whether it was proposed by the Government to intro- duce any legislative measure this session to secure comfort- able dwellings, with sufficient allotment of garden ground and proper sanitary arrangements, for cotter tenants in Ire- land.--Lord CAELisiewortu said the dwellings of Irish labourers were very miserable, but improvement must rest with the tenant farmers. The legislation now before Parlia- ment, although directly dealing with tenant rights, had an important and indirect bearing on the condition of Irish labourers. If the condition of Irish tenants could be raised so as to induce them to invest their capital on the farms, a great step in the right direction would be taken." Last week, in the House of Gammons, the Government accepted a resolution to the effect that it was desirable to improve the condition of agricultural labourers in Ireland. This showed that the Government were alive to the question raised by the noble lord.—Eventually the subject chopped. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. PRISON AND FREE LABOUR.—Sir WM. HARCOURT, re- plying to Mr. Thorold Rogers, said it was only fair to the public Who supported prisons by their taxes, that the labour of the prisoners should be sold at the highest price in the best market, and, further, the Government departments should purchase the articles they required in the cheapest market they could find. la ith regard to this competition of prison labour disturbing the larsaur market, he desired to observe that as a practical question the 14,000 persons in Prisons were withdrawn from the labour market, and would be competing with soraebody if they were at large. PATUNTS FOR INVENTIONS BILL.-Mr. ANDERSON moved the cecond reacting, of the PatPnts for Inventions Bill. Be explained that this was not an inventor's Bill. It would benefit the inventor, but would do a still greater service to the public in the way of stimulating inventive genius. The principal provisions of the Bill were the establishment of a Board of Commissioners to do the work of the Patent Office,

, an extention of the period of patents from 14 to 21 years, a reduction of fees, and a term of grace in the matter of the periodic payments.—Mr. DILLWYN admitted the desirability of amending the patent laws, but objected to the provisions ; of the Hill, more particularly the extension of patent right to twenty-one years. He moved the rejection of the Bill.— Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, whilst criticising the Bill, acknowledged the necessity of reform. It was, however, he thought—and the remark was approved by general cheering—a subject which the Government should take up. He could not pledge the Government to any particular time for dealing with the' matter, but he looked forward with pleasure to an oppor-I • tnnity for irfizoducing the Bill when the House should havel resumed control over its affairs, and was able to proceed with the business of the country.—ln the long conversation which followed a general opinion was expressed in favour of reform, whilst at the same time Mr. Anderson's pro-1 Iposals were sharply criticised.—Mr. PLAYFAIR expressed{ the general opinion when he characterised the Bill as " intentioned but not effective."—Leave was given without division to read the Bill a second time, but on the general understanding that the measure would not be further pro- , ceeded with: • SALE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS ON SUNDAY (WALES) BILL.—On the motion to go into committee on the Welsh Sunday Closing Bill, Mr. Causurr moved, as an instruction to the committee, that Monmouthshire should, for the pur- poses of the Bill, be regarded as a part of Wales. This was rejected by the ATTORNEY-GENERAL, and negatived without a diviehin, On the motion that the Speaker leave the chair, Mr. WanYox moved the rejection of the, Bill. This was supported by Mr. P. A. TAYLOR in a racy speech, in the course of which he attributed the authorship of the Bill to . , "the party of conscience virtue," a party consisting partly of Sabbitaritins and partly of teetotallers, whose object ,wae to cut off from the poorer portions of the,cornynunity odd portions of their little,enjoyments. The motion to go into committee was carried ,by 123 votes against 29. Sir Haw LANCIE GIFFARD then waved that Cardiff be excepted from the operation of the Act. On this the committee divided, and it was rejectedby 118 votes against 27. The Bill,then passed through committee, with the addition of an amend- ment providing that nothing in the Act should preclude the sale at any time at a railway station of intoxicating liquors to persons arriving ,at or departing from such station by railway'. The retnaining orders were disposed of, and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIIIESDAY. Taaitbiuspj tic ENGLAND.—The Earl of DARTMOUTH called attention to the case of John Gateley, the Irishman who was shot dead at Solihull, near Birmingham, in December last. His lordship said that though he did not with to attribute motives, he considered that the strong ex- pressions used during the electoral campaigns in Lancashire and Midlothian, must have led some persons in the astir island to consider that outrage and violence would have the effect of bringing certain ques- tions 'lvithin. the range of practical politics.—The Earl of DaLlionsm, in reply, said that he had had some difficulty in discovering the object of the noble lord's notice, but he now found that it was an ingenious method llof making an attack on Mr. Gladstone's speeches in Mid- lothian. As to the tragedy which had been made the ground for this attack, the coroner said the evidence was equally oonalstent With mnrder of accident, and before his death Gateley had told the priest that he believed the affair was the result of accident. The Married Women's Property (Scotland) Bill passed through committee.—The Fugitive Offenders Bill was read a third time and passed. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tnurisnay. THE TwassvAAL.—Sir M. Hicks-Beach asked the Prime Miniater whether the time had now arrived when his motion with respect to the Transvaal could be discussed without injury to the public service.—Mr. GLADSTONE replied that it would not have been the choice of the Government to have invited at such a time a discussion upon the affairs of the Transvaal; but, considering the nature of the demand and the quarters from which it proceeded the Government would not feel themselves justified in offering any objection to the discussion, and they would therefore be prepared, after they had heard of the completion of certain opera- tions now in progress, to make a tolerably definite arrange- ment.

OUR TRADE WITH FRANCE.—Mr. WIVEE asked the President of the Board of Trade if he would furnish a brief statement showing theyalue of the exports to and imports from France.—Mr, CHAMBERLAIN said he had no objection to make an extract of the particular figures desired by the hon. member, if the hon, member thought it well that they should be published. He might tell him, however, that it would show that the suggestions contained in this question were not consistent with the facts. A LIVELY DISCESSION.—Sir if. D. Wolff and Lord R Churchill provoked a warm and disorderly discussion by demanding an immediate answer to the question whether °the British Consul bad access to the Rev of Tunis on public matters, and on failing to obtain the information moving the adjournment of the House. The Prime Minis- ter was disposed to recommend the House to go to a division in orde • to mark its disapproval of the action of Sir H. Wolff, but ultimately the hon. member for Portsmouth was allowed to withdraw both the motion fertile adjournment and the I demand for an immediate answer to his question. The House then resumed committee upon the Land Law (Ireland) Bill at the 26th line of the first clause.

THE WARR NGTON OVERSEERS ND THEIR DUTIES. At the n• ntbly meeting of die overseers of Warrington _ _ held last ty, Mr. H. Kent presided, and there were also present Messrs. G. BlsckltdhM. Bowden, A. Mackie, and J. L. Tunstall (deputy assistant overseer). The minutes stated that on the 27th ult. the assistant overster wasisstructed to ascertain as far as possible the rentals of the various holdings in Arpley meadows, and to fix the as- sessment accordir.gly.—Mr. BLectunnar asked how many ' assessments there were in Warrington.—Mr. TIINSTALL said about 8,000; lee could not guess the exact number.—Mr. BLAcirmintse, : Does the 8,000 represent Warrington and Latchford P—Mr. 'lstrwsrAtz : I have nothing to do with Latchfard.—Mr. Bucturansr : Can you give us any idea how many have been re-assessed out of these B,ooo.—Mr. Turrerm: About 600.—Mr. BLAcwirnitsr: Only 600 with all the shops, public-houses, and works 7—Mr. TmesTALL: That is all.—Mr. BretatHußsr : It is a most extraordinary thing if that is ao.—The CHAIRMAN I just happens in this form—if, in going through the list of assessments, there are only 80 many want altering, no matter how many thousands there are, you just have to mention those which are altered. —Mr. Tom/TALL: A great many more have been con- sidered, of course—Mr. BratexcHvrarr : That is what I want to know. Only 600 have been re-assessed, but how many have been passed as being correct ?—Mr. TIINSTALL : I should think a cosple of thousands.—Mr. BLACK- Hirasilair agitteinent made to the Assessment Committee, the previous week, that was very startling. Mr. Tunstall said there were thousands of assessments which he had laid before the overseers, that were under assessed, that they would not deal with. That was the question he wanted to deal with. When a man talked about thousands it was startling.—The CHAIRMAN: It means thousands of these cases have not been gone into.—Mr. BLACKHIIRST Do .vou conaider everyone not dealt with under assessed? If so, what have the overseers and the Assessment Committee been doing? It would appear they have been doing nothing at all.—Mr. TONSTALL lam prepared to substantiate what I have stated.—The CHAIRMAN said a re-assessment took place from two causes—one from an increased, and the other de- creased value.—Mr. Bractuuusr : 11 property be decreased in value, how can it be under assessed P—The CHAIRMAN: I don't understand it at BLACENURNr Then yyetet: are very, stupidl—The erdittarant : I Always was, and keen enough to perceive ,it I—Mr. &Amman' : Mr. Tunstall told the committee there were thousands of cases under assessed, do you understand that,—The CHAIR- MAN : Yes.—Mr. &Acumen : Very well, if a house is under , assessed, it can't ,be over assessed, and can't be . in the thousands . The CHAIRMAN: You know very well Mr. Tunstall prepared a list and submitted it to this Board, but in going into that list, and from what you had heard outside, you refused to take the Bet as it then stood.—Mr. litLacisarrasr : Because the first page I turned over was to my mind wrong.—Mr. Blackhurst further stated that a great deal of the property in dispute, was cottage property, and had been built within the last eight years.—Mr. TutiErraLL said a great portion of the property was old property.—Mr. BLACHHIIRST : A great' portion has been built in the last eight years. Very well, I take it that the assistant overseer assessed it according to the rentals and the value of the adjoining propet ty. Since then property has depreciated in value and rents have gone down and how is it these houses are under assessed now 7—Mr. TuNrrALL: It is quite impossible for me to say what was done seven or eight years ago. I have not been here seven or eight years.—Mr. BLACKHIIRST said it was a misfortane that they had not the responsible person present.—The CitatuirAN said Mr. Tunstall was responsible for any state- ment he made. Mr. TUNSTALL : If you are preparedto count the agitessntents I will lay them before you. It is the only 'way in „which ray statement can be verified.—Mr. MACKIE said it was scarcely to be expected they would count the assessments. Mr. Tunstall had brought 11 little hooks before them; did thine contain thousands P—Mr. Terwerata. : Yes they do.—Mr. Keens: Can you tell us how many thousands ?—Mr. Tmesratm: Ishould not like to do that.— ,131.aptlinnsT; But we should like tp.know. Do you mean to taloa if we revised all these books we should find a thouiand under assesaed ?—Mr. TuNsTALL: Yes, above two thousand.—Mr. Bowden: The first statement made when that book was brought was that the number of eases was 1,500 or I,Boo.—Mr. Truasverm: There were 1,800, 25 p.c. wrong. You asked me to prepare a list of those which were 35 p.c. wrong, and those amounted to 1,800 ;'and it stands to reason there Moat be a great many more which are under 25 p.c. wrong.—The CHAIRMAN: Yes, that will make it thou. sands.—Mr. TIINSTALL said if they would allow him to say a few.words he would be able to show, from information which he hail laid before the overseers, that the estimate had been pretty accurate, although it had been called "guess- work. The number of appeals which had been heard by the Assessment Committee in the 12 months immediately preceeding the last meeting, was 557, and the amount' of return made by the Assessment Committee was.. £3,351 109., oof amount £3,124 10s. was allowed on property which had not been increased at all, and the balance of £227 only was remitted by the Assessment Committee on assessments which had been in- creased. Considering that the amount of increase was something like £6,000 or £BOOO, he thought that showed the information must have been pretty accurate.—The CHAIR- sus said the figures showed the assistant overseer had been near the mark.—Mr. &Amman did not see very much in it.—Mr. Bownxte said in the report of the discassion at the meeting of the Assessment Committee it seemed Major Cartwright asked whether the overseers had power to reduce the assessments, and the Chairman replied to the effect that the overseers had no power to reduce any assessment.—Mr. TUNSTALL said the question referred to works.—Mr. BLACK- HURST thonght if the overseers' proceedings had been pro- perly put before the committee, they would have been spared the remarks that were made, because it was a well-known fact that the overseers had the interest of the ratepayers as much at heart as the committee. It was also a well-known fact that the overseers, 'previous to this year, had taken no part whatever in the, consideration of these cases. They had left them entirely to the assistant overseer, and simply came there to sign what he had done almost without asking a queition.—The CHAIRMAN: Well, I'm surprised at you saying so because you are an old overseer.—Mr. BLACK- HURST fell so strongly that be had fully made up his mind what he would do. He was heartily sick of the position they were in. They simply came there to endorse what was done; but he did not feel inclined to be in that position any longer, and before he gave his sanction to raise any assess- ment whatever he should 'certainly satisfy kimself that the assessment was right.—The CHAIRMAN was astonished at Mr. BLAcirHunsT, as he was an old member.—Mr. BLACK- HURST : I have stated a fact.—The CHAIRMAN: And I say your statement is as incorrect as it could possibly be, and is an insult to the old overseers.. You never knew a case in your life of the old overseers raising or reducing an assess- ment brought before us but we discussed the matter. We never did and never hare taken what the assistant overseer did.—Mr. BLACKFIIIRST : My. experience is different,— The CHAIRMAN: lam astonished. How did it happen that you as an old member never 0110 e intimated you were dis- satisfied, but gave your sanction when the thing was pro- posed ?-31r, BLACKHURST : I never was satisfied.—The CHAIRMAN: You ought to have said so. You'did not act as you ought to have act-ed.—Mr. Bownsw said be had not sought election, but baying been elected, he had come into that office with a determination to do his duty as far, he knew it. But he objected to the way in which the over- seers had already been treated by the deputy assistant over- seer. He did not expect anything more than what was expected from any servant, but he must decline te be spoken to in the manner in which they had been on several occasions. He maintained that the overseers had not re- fused to deal with the assessments—(hear, hear)—but they refused to put their signatures to a list which they had not examined.—Mr. MACKIE said it certainly appeared before the committee as though the overseers bad been in the habit of passing anything put before them.—The CHAIRMAN said- through the sickness of the assistant-overseer a great deal of the work was in arrear, but Mr. Tunstall had done every- thing he could to work them up. He blamed the chairman of the Assessment Committee for being too harsh on the overseers, as he must know when work got in arrear it took some time to work it up.—Mr. MACKIE could not refrain from stating that the position Mr. Tunstall had placed the overseers in before the Assessment Committee was an unfair one. The overseers had not had time to do the work they were asked to do.—After some further discussion, the Chairman and Mr. Mackie were appointed a deputation to wait upon the Assessment Committee at the next meeting.— Mr. TuNsTALL explained that he was not there as a mere clerk but was engaged by*Mr. Pilling as a public accountant to perform his duties while sick. He thought it very unfair to say without just cause that his work had not been pro- perly done because he maintained the work had been pro- ' perly done.—Mr. MACKIE said Mr. Tunstall's position would have been much more pleasant had he adopted a different' tone.

LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, THRBSDAY.—Beef is firmly held, and pork remains steady in value. Fresh landed parcels of bacon are In some request; others • very dull. Hams meet still an active inquiry. Shoulde s command late priixa. Cheese has a good consumptive demand. Butter again closes fiat. LIVERPOOL CORN, TIIIIIMAT —There is very little doing here in wheat, and quotations are nominally un,•hanged. Flour In small demand at former prices. Mixed American Indian corn remains in imbed roam t at unaltered rates; we quote new at 4s lid and old at 4s ilfd to Is per cental. Beaos very firmly held for extreme figures. Peas quietly steady.. Oats ' and oatmeal continue very dull. Loynott, DEAD NIE&T, THITESDAM —Beef trade continues fiat; other descriptions meet a quiet sale, with moderate sup- plies. Beef, 2s 4d to 4s 4d; prime scotch ditto 0 41. to 4s. 81 ; mutton, 3s 4d to Sc; veal. 4s 8d to 58 4,13 lamb, 78 to Sc; large pork. Sc 81 to is 41; small pork, 0 vid to 4s 101 per Site , CORK BUTTER, THURSDAY.—Ordinary ; Firsts, 104 s; seconds, 975; thirds, 89t; fourths 85s; fifths 40s; superfine, 113 s; fine mild, 106 s ; mild. 975. Salt Kegs Firsts, 1048; secodd 973; thirds. 85s. Number of firkins; 2,051. MANCHESTER COTTON, Tartesnev.-z-Oloth is firm, but not more arrive than yestetday,'. while yarns are tn'we freely offered for sale in some quarters, spinners finding it •necessary to abandon their late high quotations. The day brought no change With it as it advanced. Goods were well sustained as to price, but little business was dos* In therrt. Yarns con- tinned to show a drooping tendency wherdver orders were at all in mqiiest, and have now praetdeally. lost almost all they have gained since the end of May. LIVERPOOL COTTON, THURSDAY.—The spot demand con- tinues m .derate, and the general tone of the market Is dull; prices, however, are without quotable change. Egyptians are exceptionally raised id per lb in the medium grades. Arrivals opened steady with buyers at yesterday's closing rates, but afterwards became easier and declined 14341 to I-32d per lb in the near mi nth-, distant, being without changed. A partial recovery took place before the receipt of the New 'York advices, which was afterwards lost, and the market closed dull. Pow York opened steady, at six points decline. The second report was "Barely steady, two mints further decline; receipts, 3.600 bales." Ihe sales are estimated at 8,000 bales, including 1,000 on speculation and for export.
