div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

On Saturday, at Foresters Hall, London, two meetings, attended by about 1,200 postal telegraph employds of both sexes, the president (a senior clerk) contradicted the state- ments of the rostmaster-General in the House of Commons with regard to overtime being balloted for. Other speeches were delivered, and it was put to the vote whether the men and women would agree to strike if this course of action were decided upon. A reply was given in the affirMative, and a resolution embodying the determination was unani- mously agreed to. Resolutions were also passed calling a national conference of telegraph clerks, to be held in Liver- pool in three weeks time, and pledging the meeting to abide by the decision of the conference. It was also resolved to take immediate steps to bring about a total cessation of overtime work.

At a confirmation at St. Philip's Church, Birmingham, last week, the Bishop of Worcester confirmed Mr. William C. Thomas, who has been for five years an Independent minister. Mr. Thomas is to be ordained. CONTEMPLATED MARRIAGE OF MR. HERBERT GLAD- STONE.—The Yorkshire Post London correspondent under- stands that Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P. is about to be mar- ried to a daughter of the late Lord Huntingtower, sister of the present Earl of Dysart, and granddaughter of the late earl, who for many years lived a secluded life in a street between the Strand and the Thames. An Irish American, named Flynn, was charged at the Liverpool Police-court, on Tuesday, with recklessly firing a revolver in a crowded thoroughfare. He was drunk, and while passing along the street he pulled out a revolver and commenced firing. One. bullet whizzed close by a police- man's head. After he had, fifeg the second shot be was arrested and the revolver taken from him, It contained seven chambers, five being loaded with ball cartridge. The prisoner was very violent. He was fined 205., or fourteen days.

At the meeting on Thursdav, of the Lancashire and Cheshire Association of Baptist Churches an address, in the form of a circular letter, to the churchei was read by the Rev. Hugh Stowell Brown, of Liverpool. The special sub- ject dealt with by the rev, gentleman was "Christianity in relation to patriotism." A resolution was passed expressing satisfaction at the passing of the Burials Act, supporting the Government "in its patriotic and Christian attempt by means of their Land Bill to redress the wrongs from which _ . . _

tillers of the soil in Ireland have suffered for 'many gener; dons," and assuring the Premier and Chief Secretary of the sympathy of the members of the Association. The meeting also express,d its opinion by resolutions on the Sunday Closing Bill and other matters.

THE WANT OF CHU/3ES.—R is surely worth our while to inquire what is the fate of the baby, or rather of the thousands of babies whose mothers are compelled by neces- sity to leave their homes and work for a living. How is it with the little ones who live in the back slums of our large cities, where families are crowded by the score into one house, the young are exposed to every bad influence, health is sapped by foul air and unventilated rooms, while, to add to all other troubles, the mother is obliged to be absent? Ucfortunately in too many cases there is no doubt about their fate, and it a sad one. Of course, something must be done with the babies who are left without a Mother's care. Sometimes they are locked up alone in the miserable homes, with just as much food as will keep them alive; 'sometimes they are left in the care of an elder sister, who is herself little more than a baby, and who, though wonderfully clever and cute for her age, as poor children frequently are, ls physically unfitted for the task devolving upon her. Mote frequently still, they are given into the charge Of one of those women who make a living by taking babies for hire while their mothers are away. The evils associated with fhb' latter method are too well known to need description

- --- here. The babies are too often dragged and soothed in order to prevent their giving trouble, until their health Pr completely ruined,and their feeble hold of life is loosened.— From "Zhe Quiver" for June.

The fortnighlly meeting of the Board was hell at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, Mr. John Ashton in the chair. There were also pres,nt:—Rev. J. W. 21: Tanner, Messm. Charles Rigby, Henry Lowe, John Mclntyre, Hy. Stringer, Thomas Andrews, John Challoner, Joshua Midwood, Mark Mounfleld, 'Jas. Derbyshire, John Weir, Charles Moen&ld, , Henry Neild, Charles Reynolds, William Jackson, William Pickering, J. W. Baguley, Thomas Norman, G. S. [Late- hurst, William Handley, and John Highlield. PAYMENT FOR EXTRA SERVICES. The CLERK bad received the following letter from the Local Government Board, dated June 3rd :—" I AEI directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 23rd ult., and to inform you that, in pursuance of article 172 of the general order of.the 24th July, 1847, they approve of the payment,to you by the Guardians of the Runcorn Union, of the sum of £I2 I2s. in consideration of the extra services which you rendered under the Union Chargeability Act during the past year. THE BOARD AND SUNDAY CLOSING. The CLERK submitted a petition against the sale of in- toxicating liquors on Sunday, which he had received from the Central Association for stopping the sale of intoxicating liquors on Sunday.— Mr. CRALLONER moved, and Mr. MIDWOOD seconded, that the clerk be instructed to prepare a petition against the sale of intoxicating liquors on Sunday, and obtain the signature of the chairman of the Board and forward it to Parliament—The Chairman seemed to have some objection to signing the petition.---A MEMBKR said if the Chairman objected to signing the petition he did not see why every member should not sign it.—Mr. CHAr.a.osma : It ought to be signed.—THE CHAIRMAN thought it required some consideration, and it would be time enough if the mat- ter was brought forward at the next meeting.--Mr. LowE said they probably would not have so good a meeting on the next occasion.—The CHAIRMAN said there was a good deal to b- said for and against the closing of public hotmes on Sun- days. The workingman would not be able to get his glass as he could not keep wine or a barrel.—Mr. CHALLONER : He can get it in a bottle.—A MEMBER :He must get it on the , Saturday.—Another MEMBER: It will get flat before the Sunday.—Mr. CHALLONER : Canon Barclay will sign it.— The CHAIRMAN: I don't mean to say I should refuse to sign it if you pass it. I can only do it in my official capacity.—The motion was put to the meeting and carried with only two dissentients. RATES.

The CLERK reported the receipt of a precept for county and bridges rate amounting to £835 3s. 3d., as compared with £982 for the corresponding quarter cf last year. THE PROPOSED HOSPITAL EXTENSIOES.—PSELESS MEMBERS. •

The Local Government-&-ard-Kad sent an order for the signatures of the members of the Board consenting to the borrowing from them of the sum of £2,400 for the carrying out of the proposed extension of the hospital. The follow- ing estimate of the cost of the work from Messrs. C. E. Linaker and S. Davies was read :—" Frodsham, Preston Brook, Cheshire, 13th June, 1881.—To the Guardians of the Runcorn Union.—Below we give you estimate for extension of hospital, in accordance with the plans, as approved by the Local Government Board. The estimate is in excess of what was at first intended, but is as low as it can possibly be brought to provide the accommodation required by the authority, viz., for 70 inmates, as against 38 at present; and having in view the building regulations of the Local Govern- ment Board. In conseqnence of having to construct the w.c.'s and lavatories as projections from the main buildings, which greatly increase the cost, and the provision of extra accommodation for nurses in cases of emergency, the area of each main building is increased considerably. When carried out the arrangements will be very convenient and complete. Estimated cost, exclusive of hot water pipes, £2,370 6s. 10d.— Mr. Nosatew observed that under the amended-plans extra accommodation would be afforded for 32 patients.—Several members eirpressed surprise at the amount of money needed. —The CLERK said the Local Government Board had stated the accommodation was insufficient, and asked the Board to take down the present hospital and put up a new one, which they estimated would cost £4,100. Tae Board resisted th at, and sent plans to the Local Government Board which were not approved, certain alterations being made which increased the cost.—The CatAtsmAN: I suppose that this will last about 30 or 40 years P—The CLEsts : Yes. He add ad that all their loans were now clear.—Mr. Norma); said it was much better to carry out the alteration properly than have to increase it again in four or five years. The expenditure seemed large but the repayments were only something like £l2O a year. The carrying out of the plans as at first drawn up would only have entailed an expenditure of £1,600 or £1.700, and in estimating the cost of the proposed altera• Cons at £2,370, they did not say it would cost that sum. That would depend upon the tenders.—The CLERK remarked that several other works which they had had done had been carried out for less than the estimated cost. (Hear, hear.)—lt was unani- mously agreed that the alterations should be made ;.and the members signed the form of consent sent by the Local Government Board. It was then discovered that it was requisite that a majority of the members, including ex- •officios, should be obtained, and that a sufficient number was not present. —The CLERK said there were' 115 ex-officio mem- bers, and for the last three years they bad but made two visits, and these were both made by the same member. (Laughter.)—Mr. Lows: We ought to strike them off.— Mr. ANDREWS : They are of no use. Write to the Local Government. Board and tell them they are of no use.-1 he CHAIRMAN suggested that the consent of the Local Govern- ment Board be obtained to obtain the signatures outside the Board —Mr. HANDLEY moved that the Clerk write to the Local Government Board asking for permission to get the corder for additions to the Workhouse signed by the Guar- dians and ex-officio members of the Board at any time than at meetings of the Board.—Mr. Jourr MCINTYRE seconded the motion, which was carried. THE SCHOOL QUESTION AT FRODSITAIL The CLERK said the School Attendance Committee ad- journed to Frodsham to go into the Frodsham case, and he had drawn up a draft letter to be forwarded to the Education Department in reply to their complaints. It was as follows :—" I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your letter, dated 21st ult., complaining of the irregularity of attendance in Frodsham schoolsond inquiring what steps the committee had taken to enforce the bye-laws, and what number of summonses Mid been isaned under them, and with what result. I ..nt qirected to inform you that the bye- lows were received from the Education Department on the 14th January last, and they were duly reported to the School Attendance Committee at the next ordinary meeting, held on the Bth February, 1881, when they were ordered to be Publieh•ed in placard form, and copies furnished in pant- phleta to the school attendance officers. These preliminaries occupied the month of February, and the operation of the bye-laws only therefore took effect during two months of the school year mining April, 1881. The committee have since held five sittings, and in addition W formal warnings, have ordered legal proceedings to be taken in 12 cases for noncompliance with school attendance orders, and in 32 cases far violation of bye-laws. The above proceedings are pending in many cases, as the petty senors are held m lathly in the rural district of the committee, including the township of Fmdsham and Frodsbam Lordship. The school attendance officer of then odsham district during the year ended 31st December, 1880, reported 174 cases to the com- mittee for investigation, and issued warnings to 44 parents in respect of 81 children. Ile also obtained school attendance orders for 6 children, and secured convictions sgaiust nine parents in rospect of 19 child, en for non-compliance with school attendance orders. In the same district committal orders were issued against five parents for non-payment of fines, and in two cases the parents went to prison in default. lam therefore directed to enclose a copy of report made by Mr. Riley, school atten- dance officer of the Frodsham district, in reference to the complaint made by H.M. inspector respecting the Frodsham schools. I have the honour to be, sir, your most obedient servant, HENRY LisragEn.—The School "Attendance Officer had reported as follows: Dear air, I have to acknowledge the receipt of letter from the Education Department, dated May 21st, 1881,calling attention to the irregular attendance at the Frodsham schools, and asking to be informed what steps had been taken to enforce the bye-laws, and bow many sum- monses had been issued under them. For the information of the School Attendance Committee,' beg to report as fo,lows : The bye-lawn were passed by the committee on the sth Oct., 1880, and approved by Her .Majesty In council 16th Dec, 1880. They were received from the Education Department 14th Jaunatv, 1881. Theg were posted in placard form Felaimary 18th, and on the 28th February copies in pamphlet form were forwarded to the,school attendance officers. It will be seen that, according to the above dates, only two months bad elapsed when the bye-laws could be said to be really in force to the end of April, when the school year OOPS in Frodsham; therefore, under the circumstances, I consider the report of Her Majesty's inspector somewhat premature. As to the steps that have been taken to enforce the bye-laws, I lave to state that no summonses have at 'Present been issued under them in this district. I have reported a considerable number of irregular children to the committee since the bye-laws came into force, and under their instructions have served the parents with a warning and also s copy of the bye-laws. In some cases there has been an improvement, but the majority of them I shall re- port again to the committee at their next meeting and ask for authority to serve summons. I desire to point out to the committee the inconvenient place where the petty ses- sions are held, namely, at Oakmere, a distance of 8 miles from Frodsham. lhe inhabitants of Frodsham and neigh- bourhood have memorialized the justices to establish a petty sessions at Frodsham, but no notice appears to have been taken of the memorial. If the committee could in any way be instrumental in inducing the justices to comedy, I feel asaure I that the enforcement of the bye-laws would be then ',loch easier of accomplishment.—Yonrs truIy,TROMAS RILEY."-1t was unanimously agreed that the letter drawn up by the clerk should be forwarded to the Education De- part ment

EXPLOSION ON BOARD A NEW STEAMER AT BARROW.-- The steamship City of Rome, built for the Inman Company for the Atla tic trade, was launched at Barrow, on Tuesday. Next to the Great Eastern, the vessel is the largest cteamer aflat. The launch was made the occasion of a gmersl holiday in Barrow and neighbourhood, and many thowarale af persons assembled to witneas the proceedings. About an hour before the ceremony of naming the Vessel, which was performed by Lady Constance Stanley, the boiler of a donkey engine on board exploded, killing two men and la youth and injuring seven other workmen. So great was tie force of the explosion that the boiler was thrown 100 yards away, and one of the men was blown off the ship into the yard, a distance Of 50 or 60 feet. The cauae of the explo- sion has not yet been ascertained.

_ A WIDNES BANKRUPTCY CASE. At the London Bankruptcy Court, on Tuesday, an appli. I cation was made to Mr. Registrar Pepr, sitting as chief judge for an order settins as:de an .njunctim against Mr. Rock liquidatw of the Alien Alkali Works at Widnes from at. tching a legacrdue to the debtor, It appeared that the debtor, who was described as a shipbroker's clerk, 58, Spur- stowe-road, Hackney, and late of Farnworth, near Warring- ton, was the late secretary and e contrioutory to the Albin Alkali Company, and on the 31st May last presented a peti- tion for liquidation, with debts to the amount of £6,000, for the most part due in Liverpool. On the Ist of June Mr. R. W. Chandler, Rine-street, Cheapside, was appointed receiver, and an injunction was granted against the liquidipter of the company.—Mr. Winslow, Q.C., for the applicaole .'• -that the Albion Alkali Company WAS formed in lerk " ..I. being at that time a shareholder to tile extent of ,t St. In 1873 the company was voluntarily wound up under the direction of the Chancery Division of the District Registry of Liverpool.and the number of contributories was fixed, Stoddart being among the number. He was served with an order to pay the calls, bat he did not obey it, and a writ was issued for the sequestration of his property. The amount of the money recovered under the order that had been ob- tained was £5O, which left the amount of £950 still due. In the course of this year 1881, the debtor's uncle, John Atkin, late of Liverpool, died, leaving a legacy to his nephew, under his will dated the 29th Nov., 1879, ef £5OO, and the debtor Nile]. When the liquidator heard of this windfell he brought an action in Liverpool to attach it, and wasire- strained by the Bankruptcy Court.—The learned conesek, after referring at c tnsiderable length to the atfidavitalp the matter, and to the authorities on the case, submitted /tat Mr. Rock was clearly entitled to be paid out of the. legacy. I —Mr. Mears, on the other side, considered that if theekieli- ' cation were allowed, it would be simple giving to theAlbton Company practically the whole of the available aged* of the debtor, and upon the Act, rule" and authorities-11'01mb. 1 mitted that one creditor could not receive the assets ',in a failure in preference to any other of the creditors, brit i that they. must share and share alike. He hoped the leartiedne- gistrar would agree with hini and dismiss the applicadon. —The learned Registrar, in givieg, judgment, was of Opeittlea that Mr. Rock, baying pursued the course that he tookrand having done all that he could to perfect his title, was in the 1 position really of a secured creditor, and, as such, of coarse he had a prior claim to the other creditors who were unse- cured, and that being so, he would allow the application and dissolve the injunction. Under the circumstances he should not make any order as to costs. .

My Dear Friends,—The very handsome and wholly unex- Pecteel expression of goodwill on the part of the gentlemen Whose names you have kindly enclosed, has deeply touched my wife and myself. To know that we possess the confidence of so many of our friends and neighbours cannot do otherwise than strengthen our hands and cheer our hearts for future work. We have no higher ambition—if in God's good providence the many years of mutual health and strength be vouchsafed of whi..h your letter speaks—than that they should be spent in promoting Christ's cause, to the best of oar ability, in the new Diocese of Liverpool, and more especially in the Atrldeaconry of Warrington. the first official oversight of which by myself you have BO generomly remembered. A Melbourne& despatch states that the census returns for Victoria show the popula- tion of the colony to be 70,000 below the estimated number. The estimated population of this colony in June of last year was 898,452. TEE ESSENTIAL ELEMENT IN CONVERSATION.—SiECerit isy the first and most essential element in all conversation. If that be absent, though it may glitter with brilliant say- ings, all vit dity has departed from it. The habit so com- mon among men in the fashionable world of weaving some form of flattery into all their conversation with the other sex is one which every woman of true feeling will resent as an impertinence, showing only the low estimate he places upon her aelf-respect arid powers of discernment. Of all small-talk it is the smallest and the most contemptible. Real e4eem and regard hive a different ring, and she is to be pitied as a feeble dupe who cannot distinguish between the true coin and the false.

Wit wonder how long the Rev. S. F. Green, the Miles Platting Ritualistic clergyman imprisoned in Lan- caster Castle, is to be kept in gaol. Be has now been in prison nearly twelve weeks. Thirt is about double the length of imprisonment frequently indicted upon men for irleking thOir wives nearly to death, although the latter generally have to perform hard labour—a degradation which the rev. gentleman has happily been spared. It is now quite evident that Mr. Green will make no promise of obaience to the monition d Lord Penzance, and shutting" •him up in gaol and thus giving him a cheap sort of martyrdom is certainly not the way to make him. He is not im-, prisoned, it is true, because of his religious opinions, as the nitra;ldlitnelisti endeavour to msken believe, but simply for forcing upon kis congregation matters of ritual after the courts haVlorbidden him to do so. We have not the slightest --sympathy with the rev. gentles:wile religious views,- nor with thi-disobedience which be • has manifested to the court of Lord Penzanoe, *which he, as an-official of a-State Chureh, ought never to have beer. guilty of. Still the spectacle of a clergyman being ihrown into prison for an ecclesiastical offence is not to be witnessed without a sense of vain and humihation, whilst it points in an unmistakeable manner twthe only warley which such things may be avoided in future. • In -the meantime no one ca zt imagine for one moment thatillfr. Green can be kept in prison for the remainder of his days, and if the aproal to the House of Lords should go against him some way will then have to be found for releasing him, end-we think it might be found now.

Some young ladies would have declined to appear at the hymenal altar a second tirneto meet such a bridegroom, but the young damsel in question was possessed of sufficient courage to enable her to do so and I sincerely hope that she may never repent of having taken that step. I hope also that mine of my readers will be so inquisitive as to desire to know where this incident occurred, for it could scarcely be true of any of the young men in this town seeing that none of them are such ardent worshippers of Sir John Barleycorn—the records of otir police comrt will bear testimony to that. I see that considerable commotion has been occasioned in the district of Clitheroe during the last few days by the ap- pearance of a large number of Insects of a peculiar 'kind about an iach long, that eat up every bit of grass in ‘ll. very short time. The description which I have receivedvf them causes me to believe that they are very similar to the locusts or "large grasshoppers," as the Americans call them, which .are to be found in many pasts of the United States. A friend residing in Nebraska informs me that these locusts are the dread of the farmers. They frequently come up from the prairies in dense clouds making a tremendous noise as they fly along, and almest darkening the sky,so numerous are they. When the farmers see a cloud of these corning their hope and prayer isthat theymay not alight upon their corn-fields, for should they do so their crops will be destroyed, as these voracious insects devote up every green thing upon the earth, so that when they rise again the•earth appears-as if it bad been burnt.•

; &man EnTLBE HORSE AT APPLETON.-4. man -named James Brown was severely bitten by a stallion at Appleton on Tuetday. The animal belonged to Mr. Edward ' Percy, contractoroand Brown was employed as a carter by him. Having filled his cart, he was about to take hold of the animal's head.when it savagely seized- hold of iris hand with its teeth. Brown, although a powerful man, was lifted from his feet, and held up in the air as if he had teen a dog. Before he was released from his painful position the jaws of the horse had to be prized open with a-stout pieeeef wood. The driver had to visit a surgeon, mid have his wound dressed. The person who rescued bins .from‘his dangerous position was Mr. Smithson, contractor. I Tun FARMERS' ALLIANCE. —A meeting, convened by -circular, of the members of the Farmers' Alliance re- siding in the county of Chester was held at the Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe, on the.gth int.,-Mr. G. W. Latham,-of Brad- wellAiall, in the chair. A branch of the Alliance was formed, with Mr. Laroam as chairman. sad Mr. W. David- son, of Little Leigh, hon. sec. A committee was appointed representative 'of the several districts, with power to add to their number. Also collecting books were distributed to those enembers who were willing to act as hon. -canvassers and collectors of subscriptions. As there are several districts not yet represented, especiAlly Runcorn, Birkenhead, and Chester, the hon. sec. will be glad to receive the 'names of gentlemen who are willing to act in this capacity, and also those who purpose to become members.

- - LA.IYAKEL OF A RIINOORN STEAMER. —On Monday. a very fine new steamer called th "Reginald," was-launched from the shipyard of Messrs. Brandrit and Co., ,Old Quay' Runeotn. The dimensions of the vessel are, 93 feet overall, 201 t. Bin, beam, and 9ft. Cin, depth of hold. The gross registered•tonnage is 118 tons, and 'he is expected to carry 175 tons. The designs are by Mr. John S. Davies, manager and draughtsman for Messrs. Brundrit ; and Mr. rSsruuel Baker, of Oil-street, Liverpool. is the maker of the engines and boiler. The engines will be compound fiurface condens- ing—of 30 Mute nominal, and 190 effective. The vessel is the first steamer which the tfirm have built for their own trade, viz, that in Benmaevmaur sett stone, and she will run principally between that place and Runcorn. All the equipments will be of the most modern character. The launch was witnessed by a very, large nuneber of spectators, and as the vessel slipped down the ways there was immense cheering. Guns were fir, d, and a brass band under the leadership of Mr.,William Houghton' played the appropriate tune "We've swept the seas.' The steamer was taken in tow by the St. -Winifred, and berthed in th 3 Old Quay dock.

ax.—On Mewlay moles the superintendents of Camden Wesleyan Sunday School, Runcorn, presented Mr. .Jacob McQuinn, who left the town on Wednesday for the East coast, premoub-to going to Australia, on the 22nd, by the Orient line, with.a eilyer mounted dreising case. Mr. MoQuinn, has acted as secretary at the, school for upwards of.seven years, and his departure from England is much regretted. Mr. McQuinn was also connected with the Cam- den Mutual Improvement Class, of which Mr. H. Randle is the president, and the members also presented him with Sydney Smith's Historical Essays and . Leed Bacon's Social and Political Essays as a mark of their esteem. In making the presentation on behalf of the members Mr. Randle spoke of Mr.,M,cQuinn's long connection with the clam and the deep iueerestt he had always taken in its progress. He could assure them that his departure to Australia occasioned him much regret, and he heartily ,wished him every prosperity In the tar-off colony. Mr.,Shore, vice-president of the class, alsO delivered a speech to the same effect, and Mr. McQuinn baying suitably acknowledged the present, the remainder of the evening was pleas rntly spent with singing and instru- mental music. Mr. McQuinn is a young man of consider- able talent and promise; his family occupy a good position In Runcorn; ,and we have every confidence in recommend- ing him to the confidence of the Wesleyan Methodists of that part of Australia in which his lot will be cast.

TUE RUNCORN SA.Lvermx AMY', A DISAPPEKIZINCE. —A member of tte Runcorn Salvation Army, who Ims for some time acted. in an important official capacity, has sod-
denly vanishel—the place that mice knew him knows him

2152 L.R.V.—This corps had battalion drill at Widnes, on Saturday, under the command of Major Cross. There were shout 200 torn on parade. Having marched on the ground the four companies formed into line and then opened ranks for the general salute. They then marched past in column, quarter column, anti at the double. Having again formed into line they took cround to the right in fours. Having again formed into -column they left the ground in fours. Before doing so, Major Cross announced to the men that they were to be present at the coming re- view-to be held by the Queen at Windsor, which announce- ment was received with loud cheers. _Having left the Drill.

Hall, the St. Hekns companies proceeded to the station. AN ATTACK ON TUE SALVA.TION ARMY IN RUNCORN. —We hear that on Sunday night a number of the members of the Runcorn Salvation Army, who were doing some rough
missionary work at Mill Brow, were somewhat savagely attacked by a number of "fellows of the baser sort." Various stories are in circulation as to the origin and. pro-

grass of the row, and, as we understand it is very probable the case will come .before the magistrates, it may be as well not to say more ahtmiltat present. We understand the, Mr. George Crosfield, director of the London and North-Western Railway Company, has
returned film his tour of _inspection of the working of the
railway system in the United States, to which —reference
was made a short time since in these columns. ARREST OF • T•V. COLLECTOR AND ASSISTANT OVER- SEHR.—WiIIiam Boothman, till recently collector of income-

tax at Accrington, has been arrested by order of the Inland Revenue department, to be detained till the sum of £327 due to the department is paid. Boothman was also assistant ove.seer for the Haslingien Union, and it is alleged that an examination of his books has shown a deficiency of £2,480.

THE CHEESE TRADE.-A Cheshire farmer says :--The cheese trade is now in a very precarious state. Farmers in general are anxious sellers, and factors cautious buyers, chiefly owing to a much larger quantity of old being in the market than there was twelve months ago. The imports of new American being in excess of this time last year, much lower rates may shortly be expected except for the very finest descriptions, and I think there is no fear but what these will stand the severe test of all foreign competi- tion.

FOOT AND MOUTH DIEMASE. - The chief constable of Cheshire (Captain Arrowsmith) has received reports that during the past week 17 cattle had been attacked with foot and mouth disease, the epidemic having appeared on four fresh farms in the neighbourhood of Grappenhall, Lymm, Little Budivorth, and Wallasey. Twenty-eight animals out of the number already suffering from the disease had re- covered, and 35 now remain under treatment. Swine fever had attacked one animal, which bad died, in the neighbour- hood of Castle Northwich. No cases of pleuro-pneumonia

are reported. ANOTIIHR PEEsTora ELECTION Possustz. —lt is rumoured that the vacant Lord Justiceship will be offered to Sir John Holker. lam not able to say whetherthere is any truth in the report, but it is not intrinsically improbable. Though Sir John Holker is a Conservative, hie independent and straightforward political character has always com- manded the respect of his political opponente ; and it is known that Mr. Gladstone had always highly appreciated the steady and manly Conservatism which the Attorney- General has professed. It is therefore quite possible that if Sir H. games does not tare for the position, Mr. Gladstone may place the vacant. office of Lord Justice of Appeal at Sir John Holker's acceptance.—Leeds Mercury London Cor- respondent. EXTRAORDINARY WEDDING AT SOTTTRPORT.-012 Wed- nesday, the fashionable church of Holy Trinity, in Hoghton- street, Southport, was crowded to excess by persons of the lower and middle claws to witness a marriage between two well-known characters belonging to Little Ireland, a suburb of-Southport. The names of the parties are William Mar- shall, alias "Russian,"-011a3 "Gent," and Jane Monks. A woman named Ellen Toole, with whom Marshall lived for a number of years, only died a few days ago at the Ormskirk Workhouse, and Marshall now made up his mind to marry Monks. As they passed the Market Hall the stall-keepers turned out and cheered them, and probatly such a scene has not been witnessed in Chapel-street for years past. The "best man" was another person well-known to the old in- habitants, and goes under the sobriquet of " Shapeoff,'• but his proper name is Edward Marshall. The coachman's nicknames are " Powell" and "Broth," and his right name is James Rimmer. It may be stated that all the old " Sand- grounders "of Southport have nicknames, by which they, in many cases, are only known.

The 14th annual festival of the Widnes Athletic Club was held- last evening, in the show field, Farnworth-in- Widnes. During the day the weather had been of a most unpropitious character, but shortly before the commence- ment of the proceedings it cleared up, and though cool for an evening in leafy June, fairly pleasant. The attendance was not large, which was doubtless attributable to the threatening clouds which covered the horizon up to an advanced part of the afternoon. The ground, after the rain of the last few days, presented an uninviting appearance, but its damp condition did not appear to trouble the competitors very much. The committee consisted of the following gentlemen :- Messrs. C. E. Barlow, E. Bolton, Dr. Booth, E. A. Chorlton, J. H. Crossley, H. W. Deacon, D. Forster, J. Galloway, T. C. Haddock, P. B. Wade Deacon, and Major Cross. The clerks of the course: Messrs. C. E. Bar- low, D. Fenster, and A. W. Macilwaine. The handicapper and official timekeeper : Mr. Walter Platt ; hon. treasurer, Mr. James Hurst; hon. secretary, Mr. C. E. Barlow; and secretary, Mr. Jas. W. Davies. There was only a moderate attendance in the grand stand, which will, probably, be crowded to-Jay (Saturday) if the committee have their usual luck with the weather. RUNCORN WANDERERS' AND AMATEURS BICYCLE •CLUBS.—The members of these dabs, amongst whom a very good feeling exists, had a combined run to Daresbury, on Monday. DEATH OF MR. WILLIAM GILL, OF WIDNES.— Mr. Wan. Gill, of 11, Waterloo-road, Whines, collector of income tax, and formerly Conservativ., agent, died an Friday lasti after an illness of 18 weeks duration at the advanced age of 76. The deceased came to Widnes about -24 years ago, and was at one time the occupier of the Bridge Corn Mills, near to Arpley Station, War- rington, in which town he was at one film a prominent citizen. He was for many years church- warden to the late Bishop ot Soder and Man, when he was the esteemed rector of Warrington. At One time Mr. Gill took a very prominent part in town's matters in Widnes, and he was distinguished by much tact and shrewdness. During the severe weather at the early part of the year, he was seized with gangrene of the foot. Dr. McLennan attended deceased and removed the mortified por- tions of the foot ; after this had been done, at the suggestion of friends, an eminent medical man from Liverpool was nailed in, but, as above stated, all efforts to save him proved fruitless. LYII3I. LYMM LOCAL BOARD.

A special meeting of this Board was held on Thursday evening, for the purpose of considering the report of Messrs Brockbank, Wilson, and Mulliner, as to the best scheme for dealing with the sewage of the Lymm district. Mr. Cameron occupied the chair, and there were also present Messrs. Rogers, Taylor, Appleton, Richardson, Holt, Gibbon, Simpson, Hall, Ridgway (clerk), Mullard (deputy clerk), and Mort (surveyor.)

, A SEWERAGE SCHEME FOR LYMM DISTRICY.—ENGINEERS' REPORT. Mr. Wiseow attended to present the report, which stated that they had considered what would be the best scheme for the sewerage of Lymm and Statham, irrespective, as far as possible, of the special views and wishes of individual mem- bers of the Board. They had also prepared a plan to lay be- fore-the Local Government inspector at the inquiry, show- ing how the entire district can ultimately be sewered. To facilitate the arrangements for the construction of various parts of this scheme from time to time, they had divided it into distinct sections, each of which can be carried out Wren required. It is undoubtedly the best, when it can be dons, to bring the whole of the sewage to one outfall, but the levels of this district .a're such as to render this arrangement very difficult. In the scheme before the Board the engineer had left out of consideration the Rush Green and Sandy-lane sewer, which at present empties itself into the Sow Brook. This line of sewer will not be connected in any way with the scheme proposed, but arrangements can be made when necessary, by a slight alteration of the outran length, to deliver the selvage from this portion of the district on to land adjoining Sow Brook for filtration purposes. The scheme provides for the whole of the sewage being brought to one outfall; and it is the final determination of this outfall that is one of the most important features in any scheme. The character and flow of the floods to which the meadows around Statham are subject, and the general level of these meadows, which they had recently investigated, lead the engineers to the conclusion that the outfall must, if practicable, be situate to the north-west of Statham. The northerly portion of the field belonging to Captain Fex, and in the occupation of Mr. Marsh, they had fixed upon as the most suitable for these outfall works. The level of this field is about 28 feet above the ordnance datum. It is surrounded on two sides with watercourses, the water in which in ordinary times is from 3 to 4 feet below the surface of the field, and one foot lower than the water in the Statham pools. This field is 4 feet lower than Mr. Jackson's field referred to in the Board's resolution which renders it much more suitable than that field for the construction of outfall works. The portion of this field proposed to be taken for this purpose will be about five statute acres. At the south-eastern corner thereof it is proposed to construct a small tank in which the grosser materials of the sewage will be deposited. A fender or bank of earth will have to be raised round the field, the field itself being planted with osiers. The fluid matter from the tanks will flow along two channels to be constructed on the south and east of the field, from which it will find its way over the entire area of the osier bed by gravitation. In times of flood the contents of the sewers, which will be largely storm water, will be carried away by the storm overflows provided, into the natural watercourses. The population of the dis- trict proposed to be drained to this outran the engineer un- derstood to be 3,000, and the water supply about 15 gallons per head per day. Therefore in ordinary dry weather there will be flowing to the tanks 45,000 gallons per day supposing the whole of Lymm and Statham was drained. This Will be rather more than one I third of an inch when discharged over the five acres during Ithe day. They did not anticipate that the flow for some years to come would be more than one fourth of an inch I per acre. To the proposed tanks, it is proposed to bring the whole of the sewage from the south-east portion of the dis- trict, which comprises the great bulk of the population: whilst the sewage from the south-west when carried out will flow into the irrigation channel. The estimated cost of this portion of the work is £lBO, exclusive of land or road. Section No. 1 commences at the tanks and terminates at Statham-lane, and the estimated cost is £l4O. Section No. 2 will commence at Statham-lane and terminate in Whit- barrow-lane near Lymm railway station. The length will be 950 lines) yards, the main fall 1 in 356, and laid with 12 inch pipes. The average depth over nearly the whole of this length will be from 2 feet to 3 feet. About 120 yards north of Lymm railway station will be about 7 feet deep. Estimated cost, £220. Section 3 commences in Whitbarrow-lane, near Lymm station, and terminates at Lymm bridge by a junction with the exist- ing Eagle-brow sewer under that bridge The total length will be 700 lineal yards, the mean fall lin 233. Esti- mated cost £3OO. The sewer of section 4 is estimated to cost £lBO. They believed it would be found necessary to carry out the whole of these four sections at once. The total estimated cost amounts to £1,020, and 15 per cent, might be added for contingencies, making a total of about £1,200. The sewerage of the district of Lymm is provided for by section No. o, the estimated cost of which is £240. Section No. 6 is estimated to cost £6OO, No. 7 £7O, No. 8 £2OO. They had marked on the plan an alternative line by which the sewer instead of being taken across the Cow-way pit behind Statham Lodge, can be carried along the road between the Statham pools. From an engineering point of view they believed this alternative line to be feasible, but it will be necessary to construct a bridge across the pools and carry the sewer attached thereto in iron pipes. It is entirely a matter for the Board to decide as to the policy or otherwise of con- structing this bridge for the raising of the exist- ing road, which is frequently submerged at present. —Mr. TAYLon Can Ng, 1 section be gone on with without touching the others P—Mr. WiesoN: Yes.— Mr. TAYLOR: Can you do Statham without doing the others ?—Mr. WILSON : Quite so.—Having explained all the technicalities in the scheme, Mr. Wilson retired ; and the CHAIRMAN said it seemed to him a very efficient scheme and sufficient for the district. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. ROGERS : Do you propose to buy or lease the land 7—The CHAIRMAN : That is for your consideration.— Mr. RICHARDSON :1 should say buy.—Mr. HALL: Yes. Then we have it in our own hands.—Mr. SIMPSON : The question is whether Captain Fox will sell it.—The CHAIRMAN: It is well we can go before Captain Fax with a definite scheme.—Mr. HALL re- marked that from what the engineers had laid before the Board, the scheme seemed a desirable one, and the next step to take was for a deputation to wait upon Captain Fox, and arrange the terms upon which he would let them have the land.—The CHAIRMAN said he apprehended the Board had no intention of carrying out the entire scheme, and it would be a question as to how far they intended to extend the sewers at pregent.—Mr.Romts: The point to be decided is: Shall we stop at the railway station or go as far as the canal bridge.—The CHAntmAtt: It appears imperative that the work should be done.— Mr. ROGERS said that to test the feeling of the meeting he would propose that the alternative plan be adopted. The , distance was about the same as in the other, and the erection I of the bridge would settle the question of raising the road at the pools. The money to do the work could be borrowed, the repayments being spread over a number of years, and the 1 rates would not be burdened with the expense in one year. The expense would be about the same as in the other scheme.—Mr. RICHARDSON said it was not only the raising of the road, but there would have to be some protection made.—Mr. ROGERS : What difference would there be be- tween the putting up of a bridge and the raising of the road? —Mr. RICHARDSON: Consider the danger.—Mr. ROGERS : There would be less danger with the bridge than with raising the road.—Mr.lircuAnnsoN : Nonsense.—Mr. HALL made some remarks on the instability of bridges, and said that in the scheme of the engineers' there Was not the slightest risk, whilst in the other there was.—The CHAIR- MAN observed that if the Board was compelled to raise the mad, they might perhaps be able to borrow £7O or MO to do the work, instead of bearing all the expense in on lie thought, however, a bridge would be preferaeblyeeatro. raising the road. They had only a narrow basis, and if the road was raised 3 feet it would take a great quantity of rn Aerial, and it was doubtful if they could secure a sure foundation.—Mr. RICH ‘RDSON :—Are we compelled to raise the road ?—The CLERIC : As far as I know you have never been asked to do it, hut if it is not right you are bound to make it so.—Mr. Rogers' motion was not seconded, and ultimately Mr. RICHARDSON proposed that the clerk write to Captain Fox to ascertain at what price he would sell that portion of Ox Hey Meadow required for the sewerage works' and submit the plan.—Mr. TAYLOR seconded, and the motion was carried.—Mr. ROGERS moved that the outfall works, end the scheme of Messre. Brock. bank, Wilson. and Mulliner, so far as sections 1,2, 3, and 4 are concerned, be adopted, and that Messrs. Brockbank and Co. prepare the necessary plans sections, and estimates; and that the law clerk communicate with the Local Govern- ment Board relative to borrowing the money which may be required.—Mr. HALT, seconded the motion, which was passed nem con.

THE WIDENING OF STATHAM ROAD. The CHAIRMAN Said Captain Fox had agreed to let the Board have the land for the widening of Statham-road, but he could not give them the exact terms as he had not the correspandence.—Mr. Ham moved, and MT. RICHARDSON Seconded. that the work be immediately proceeded with, which was carried unanimously. The meeting then terminated. •

HOUSE OF LORDS. Thu VALUATION OF LAND.—Lord WAVENET 1101,15€1 that the. townland valuation should be adopted in all calcu- lations affecting the interests of the landlords and tenants. He concluded that the townland valuation was alone based upon a certain principle, that of the real productive value of land.—Lord LIFFORD objected to townlands being adopted as the foundation for future valuations.—Lord CARLINfI- FORD objected ta the motion and wished it withdrawn.—The motion was withdrawn. EVICTIONS FOR NON-PAYMENT OF Rmrr.—Lord Limwsucx moved for &return of the evictions for non-payment of rent since the passing of the Act of 1870, which was ageed to— Several provisional orders were advanced a stage and the House adjourned.

HOUSE OF COMMONS. THE GOVERNMENT AND LOCAL OPTION.—Sir W. LAW- SON, replying to Mr. Newdegate, stud he had full confidenee in the Government with regard to Local Option. If they did not bring in the Bill next session it would become hiS duty to consider what course he would pursue. POSTAL CLERKS AND TELEGRAPHISTS.— Mr. FewCrrn said that in a few days he would lay the new scheme on the table asregards postal clerks and telegraphists. It would increase the annual charge for the post office £150,000 per annum. TUNIS—Sir C. Dula said he had no information that the British Consul hal been refused access to the Bey of Tunis. There had been no withdrawal of any existing rights. THE NEW ARMY ORGANISATION SCHEME.—Mr. GLAa:. STONE, replying to Mr. Bartellot, said he could not fix a day for discussing he new Army Organisation Scheme. • Tux IRISH LAND Bru..--Mr. GLADSTONE hoped the amended seventh clause of the Lind Bill would be in the hands of members before the adjournment. With regard to that clause they propased to ask the committee to pass all that part of it which referred to tenant right and to a solvent tenant, and would endeavour to give directions to the court with regard to the hearing of the parties and examining all ths relative circumstances of the case. THE IRISH LAND BILL IN ComurrrEs.—The House went into committee on the Irish Land Bill.—On clause 2 which dealt with devolution of tenancies proposed, Mr. Lemon proposed to omit the latter portion of the clause.— Mr. Gransvosm objected. He said the clause would not pre- vent joint succession. It only prevented the breaking up of the tenancy.—Mr. Snew opposed that portion of the clause. —After a long discussion Mr. Lalor withdrew his proposal. —Mr. Brooms moved an amendment to the clause, to give to one of the representatives of a tenant who dies intestate or who has bequeathed his tenantry to more than one person, the right to sell if the landlord so required.—The Arronrrxx GENERAL for IRELAND opposed the amendment. A loud discussion casual For the amendment 32, against 339.-- Another amendment made was ultimately withdrawn.--. The ATTORNEY GENERAL for IRELAND moved an addition to the chnse, which would make the last section read as follows :—"Where the tenant of a tenantry dies intestate and without next of kin, such tenantry shall pass to the landlord, subject, however, to the payment of the debts and liabilities of the deceased tenant, and to the satisfaction of the claim which the widow, if any, of such deceased tenants has upon the persons' estate."—The amendment was agreed to. The clause, as amended, was ordered to stand part of the bill.—On clause three, an increase of rent to attract statutory conditions or entrance price of sale was proposed.—Mr. GLAD/NONE announced that he in- tended to move an amendment to the second sub-section in order to give a right to the landlord equal with tbe tenant to enter a court with regard to thequestion of rent, and also to confine the operation of the sub-section to future tenancies.—ln reply to Lord It. Churchill, Mr. GrAns•rom.: said he should tv-,t object as he had already said, to amend- ments being made further on giving landlords the same right to go into court as the tenant.—Sir S. Nonni- arra wished to se d the amendments on the paper before they were called on to consider them.— Mr. PARNELL condemned the amendments just announced by the Prime Minister as prejndical to the tenants and a concession to Conservative obstruction. He believed they were only the first of a series of concessions that would be made to the powerful party that opposed the Bill.—Mr. NEALE condemned the amendments announced as in favour of absentee landlords. He moved an amendment to move ommission of t ho words "present tenancy "at the commence- ment of the clause in order to give the priveleges of the clause to any tenant. A long discussion ensued.—Mr. PARNELL recommended the withdrawal of the amendment, but Mr. BIGGAR talked the amendment out and the sitting was suspended.

Another ominous discovery has been made at St. Peters- burgh. A few days ago it was announced that the Czar, not feeling safe even in his fortress palace at Gatchina, waa about to remove to Peterhoff. It is now stated thatthe whole of the officers and crew of the guardship stationed near Peterhoff have been changed on suspicion of Nihilism. A number of revolutionary proclamations have been found on board the ship. It will 1p remembered that many of the most important suspects recently arrested at St. Petersbnrg and Cronstadt were naval officers.

The telegraph clerks in the Government employ have given notice that they will cease working overtime on the 26th. The Controller has reminded them as the business of the department fluctuates largely the working of overtime is frequently a necessity; but the clerks reply, on the au- thority of Mr. Monsen (the present Lord Emly,) that over- time is not compulsory. It is announced that the clerks decided on Thursday to strike at once if any of their num- ber were suspended for refusing to work overtime. The tenants' interests in eleven farms were sold at Kil- dare, on Thursday, the tenants refusing to pay rent. Aftew a sharp competition between the representative of the Emer- gency Committee and the Land League, the full amount due from the tenants was in each case realised. After the Bahr, the Rev. Father Farrell addressed a large gathering, de- nouncing as unpatriotic thooo Irishmen who recruited the ranks of the constabulary.

During the sitting of the Lichfield Town Council, on Thursday, a sheriff's officer took possession of the Guild- hall, in which the Ineetinc.: was held. Bailiffs were placed 1 in the police office, and also at the Corporation stables. The action was taken by Messrs. Pattinson, sewerage ccntractora,. whose claim on the Corporation was for £3,500, which had been awarded to them after much litigation and on appeal. The money was paid after some hours delay. The sheriff's fees amounted to nearly £lOO.

I There left the Mersey last month 38,263 emigrants ! (22,097 of whom were foreigners), an increase of 2,623 on April last, and of 8,971 on May, 1880. The number for the ' expired five months of this year is nearly 15,060 aver that for the corresponding period of last year. REGISTRATION or VOTEILSIN rits COUNTY. —We would direct the attention of Liberals in the county to the notices affecting the registration of voters, which have been issued to overseers of the poor by the Clerk of the Peace, to be published at the respective places of worship in the townships on the 20th instant. The notices declare that no person will be entitled to have his name inserted in the list of voters in the county now about to be made in respect of the occupation as owner or tenant of lands or tenements of the rateable value of £l2 or upwards unless he shall have been the owner or occupier during the 12 months preceding . the last day of July next, and have been rated to, and shall pay on or before the 20th July next, all poor rates which have become payable by him in respect of the premises up to January sth, and all persons who omit to make such s payments will be incapable of being upon the next register. The notices also declare that all persons entitled to rote in • Parliamentary elections, in respect of any property within the respective townships, who are not upon the register now in force, or who being upon the register, shall not retain the same qualification or continue in the same place of abode as described in such register, and who are desirous to have • their names inserted in the register about to be made, art' required to send to the overseers, on or before the 20th July. a notice in writing, giving rarticulars of their qualification, name, and address.

div.p: NEWTON AND EARLFSTOWN. ATHLETIC SPORTS AT NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS. The fourth annual athletic festival of the Newton-le- Willows Cricket and Bowling Club, which was held on the cricket ground on Saturday, was highly successful in every respect. The weather was favourable, and a large number of spectators, estimated at 2,000, attended the sports. There were 14 events on the programme, and although the num- ber of entries was not so large as in previous yearso the class of competitors was good, and some capitil racing was witnessed, the dose finishes in several of the contests show- ing that the handicapper had performed his arduous task very fairly. The sports were admirably conducted, excel- ' lent time was kept, and the whole arrangements reflected the greatest credit upon the 'officials, who were as follows: —Judges : Messrs. James Fairclough, Walter Stone 8.. S. Brewis, G. Y. Bolton, Geo. Cbrke, J. R. Hillkirk, and P. B. S. Cooper; starters, Messrs. Irving and Kean; clerks of the Course, Messrs. W. Dagnall, D. Barcroft, John Ball, and 11. Ribbed ; honorary treasurer, Mr. E. Fairclough ; honorary secretaries, Messrs. T. Stone, jun., and W. D. Burdis. NEvrros Parr! SESSIONS.—At these sessions, on Satur- day, before Colonel McCorquodale (chairman), and Messrs. I Pearson, Comber Birley, and Houghton, Edward Last was I charged with with having cruelly illtreated a cow at New- ton on the 17th May.— Mr. Moore defended. —lnspector Coleman. of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, said he saw defendant strike a cow, which was in kis charge at Newton fair, a violent blow on the nose and eye, causing the cow great pain. Two witnesses were called to prove that the cow was a dangerous one, and that the blow was given to prevent it from doing injury to another animal.—Defendant was fined 50. and costs.--A similar charge was made against a farmer, named Robert Brookes, and he was fined 10s and costs.—William Tom- linson, alias John Holt, described as a collier, was charged with stealing on the 4th June a coat, a vest, and a pair of trousers, and also 20a in silver, the property of Wright Banks.—Wright Banks said the prisoner used to live with him, and on the 4th June he went to Wigan, leaving the .prisoner alone in the house. On his return he looked in his box and found that both clothes and money had been abstracted. The clothes were worth £4 ss.—Edward Raw- burst, a hawker, said that about half-past nine on Saturday night, June 4th, he was in the Cheshire Cheese Inn, off Deansgate, Manchester, when the prisoner came in carrying a bundle, and asked him if he would buy a pair of trousers. He gave him 4s. for them. He had since given up the clothes to the police.—P.C. Beardsworth, stationed at Got- borne, said he apprehended the prisoner. When charged with the theft he said, "It's no use denying it; I did it." Committed Committed for trial to the next Quarter Sessions at Liver- pool.—Thomas Bolton, a horse driver, in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Co., was charged with having. on Friday last, stolen a sack of chopped hay and a quantity of provender, value £l, from the Newton goods station, and Samuel Walton, oil merchant, Newton, was charged with receiving the same.—Mr. Preston prose- cuted on behalf of the railway company, and Mr. Riley de- fended.—Evidence having been given that the stolen goods were such as were supplied to the company by their Park- lane, depot, Liverpool.—Matthew Taylor, goods porter, Earlestown, said he saw Bolton at the station, on TuesdaY, when he told witness that he had two surplus sacks of cuonped hay, and that he should give them to Walton. On Friday Walton went and witness gave him a bag of "chop." —Henry Bradshaw, agent at the Earlestown goods station, said that on Friday morning he went to the warehouse about eight o'clock aud saw that one of the bags of provender which bad come from Park-lane on the previous Monday was gone. Shortly afterwards he proceeded to Walton's premises, taking a policeman with him. They ' found the missing sack in Mr. Walton's cellar. Walton told him he had borrowed the chop and would pay it back again. Bolton had been in the company's .employ for about ten yearn—For the defence it was contended that the goods had only been lent by Bolton, apd that he bad no intention Of stealing them.—The Bench considered that the charge had not been proved, and discharged the prisoners. PUBLIC TESSUERA.NCE MEETING AT A SHTON.—On Wed- nesday eveniag, a public temperance meeting was held in the British Schoolroom Ashton, under the auspices of the Ashton Excelsior Lodge of Good Templars. The Rev. Henry Wilson presided, and gave a hearty and encouraging address, referring to the great progress of the temperance cause during the past few years, especially in its legislative aspect. Speaking of this, he said that Sir Wilfrid Lawson's Local Option resolution calling upon the government to introduce abut, based upon such a principle, was carried in the House of Commons on Tuesday by a majority of 42. He also spoke of the probability of the Welsh Sunday Closing Bill being passed in this session of Parliament, which would go far to stimulate and encourage the temper- ance party tn work more energetically in pushing forward a similar measure for Englanl. Earnest and practical addresses were also given by Bro. R. W. Wilkins, D. Secre- tary, Bro. S. Pugh' D. Treasurer, and Bro. E. J. Freeman, DA., of Liverpool. A song was 4.180 well rendered by Bro. Freeman. The meeting closed with votes of- thanks to the chairman and speakers.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST CONFERENCE I AT HULL. On Saturday Dr. S. A,ntliff, deputy missionary teasurer, resigned that office, and his arrangement to take the super- intendency- of Derby second circuit was confirmed. The following are the appointments of ministers for this district: ' —Preston Brook: John Pickwell an Daniel Schofield; lin. Helens, Westfiekkstreet : Thomas Wilshaw ; Warrington .and Widnes: Joseph-Morton ; Skelmerstiale: William Birks; Rarlestown : Miles Dichensoa. The Conference re-assembled on Monday at Jarrattstreet Chapel, Hull, Rev. C. Kendall presiding. After the reading of memoirs of deceased members, the Conference ptoceedtd to the stationing of ministers, and appointed a committee to consider what arrangements could be made for supplying the vacancies in the different eistricts. This was strongly opposed as being contrary to connnexional rule, and a written protest was handed in, signed by about 20 delegates. The Conference adopted a petition in support of the Anti-Narcotic Leagae, the Rev. R. Cheeseman speaking very strongly against the use of tobacco especially by young people. Upen the motion of Dr. Antliff, a resolution in favour of Sir Wilfrid Lawson's local option measure was carried nnaaisaausly.—The following resolution to Mr. Cillfidstone was carried enthusiastically: The Primitive Methodist Conference, Clowes Chapel, Hull, June 13,1881. To the flight Hon. WE. Gladstone.. Sir,—We, the members and friends .of the Primitive Methodist Conference, now bolding its. sittings in Hull, and representing a Connexion of Protestant Christian Churches extending to almost all part of the United King- dom, to Canada and many of the other colonies, and to Western and Southern Africa, beg most respectfully to express to you our deep sympathy in the arduous and im- portant Parliamentary work in which you are now engaged, and in the formidable difficulties you are called upon to encounter, and to inform you that we are watching with great interest the progress of the measures you have intro- duced, and have now in hand, for the settlement of compli- cated questions in connection with our foreign relationships, and especially for the pacification of Ireland, which, we regret to learn, is in such a disturbed state. We fear that the heavy and incessant strain which, along with the other Ministers of Her Majesty's Government, you are now under, considering the advanced stage of life at which you have arrived, may prove to much for your remaining strength. Wa fervently pray that it may please the Great DispoSer of all our affsirs to preserve your life and health during Hie pressure of the present Session of Parliament, and that In the order of Providence you may accomplish the good which we are sure you have in view. The reaolation was signed on behalf of the Conterenoe by tos president and secretary.

---- ..,. A LANDLORD BRUNIE ON HIS OWN PREMISES.—John Ellis, the landlord of the Foresters' Arms publichouse, was summoned for being drunk on his own premises, on the 30th ult.—P.C. Bossorts said that about twenty minutes to seven on the evening of the day named he was going along Canal- street, when he saw the defendant, who was drunk. He next observed him walk into the vaults, and in a few minutes he followed him. Ile then saw that he had fallen on to the floor, in a helpless state of drunkenness.—Defendant was fined ss. and costs, 9s. 6d. THE Smoot. Boann AT WORE.—The following parents had each 55., including costs, to pay for not sending their children to school:—Daniel Wellington, John Inman, Peter Johnson, James Giter, Thomas Woodfine, Ann Whitley, Michael Kenyon, Mary Rawlinson, and Michael Rogers.— i The cases were proved by Mr. Bowyer, school attendance officer. It was expected that the question in dispute be- tween Mr. Ashton, the magistrates' clerk, and Mr. Rigby, the School Board clerk, as to what is necessary to constitute an authority to prosecute on the part of Mr. Bowyer, would have been argued, but as the request of the magistrates had been acceded to by Mr. Rigby, the point did not arise. ASSAULT ON A BOY BY A NAVVY:A navvy named Michael Rogers, employed on the railway extension at Birdswood Junction, was charged with assaulting a lad named Thomas Gibbons, on the 2nd inst.—About 70 navvies are working on the spot named, and the complainant was engaged to carry meai and water to them. He had supplied a gang in which defendant worked, and was taking seine to a second company, when Rogers went up to him and asked for another supply. He was told he could not have it until the other men were served, on which he hit the youth on the head with a small can which he (Gibbons) was carry- ing, and also threw a large piece of marl at him which hit him On the side and caused him considerable pain.—De- fendant said he 'did not touch complainant until he had threatened to strike him with a piece of twisted wire.—He was ordered to pay a fine of 10s., and 12s. 6d. costs, and in default to be sent to gaol for 14 days—Defendant: I will go to prison. WHIT-MONDAY'S AMUSEMENTS IN ARTHUR-STREET.— Mary Perry, a married woman, was charged with assaulting Mary Johnson, of Arthur-street, Newtown, on Whit-Monday. —Complainant stated that there was a row in the street, and as she stood at her own door, the defendant came up and struck her in the face.—James Orme, Wm. Pritchard, and Kate Rathbone gave corroborative evidence—Defend- at said two men attacked her husband, kicking him, and on running out to help him, complainant seized her by the hair.—Sarah Whittaker and Martha Gerrard corroborated. --Another case was then heard, in which Thomas Perry the husband of the defendant in the previous case, was charged with assaulting Mary Walsh, a young woman.— Complainant said that, without any provocation, defendmt struck her in the breast as she was going up some steps in the Holloway. Walter Joynson gave corroborative evi- dence, and said defendant was the terror of the neighbour. hood.—The defembn's in each case were bound over to keep the peace for six months, themselves in £lO, and two sureties in $.5 each. They also had the costs to pay. • TurrnSaay.—Before Mr. A. Thomas (chairman) and Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst. THEFT BY A Lan.—lsaac Johnson, aged 13, was charged with stealing a shirt, a towel, and a tablecloth, the property of Samuel Rodda, on the 14th inst.; and also with receiving the articles knowing them to have been stolen. Mary Rodda, wife of the prosecutor, who lives at Wivern-place, said that Tuesday was her washing-day, and about a quarter past one in the afternoon, she hung the things which the prisoner was charged with stealing on a line upon a piece of land near to Potter's premises. in Canal-street. She missed them between two and three' and went to Mr. Imison's pawnshop, Church- street, to give him notice about the robbery. She was sent for to the shop shortly afterwards and found the prisoner there with the stolen articles.—Mr. unison said that on the prisoner bringing the things to pawn, he asked him who bad sent him, and he said his mother.—After some evidence by the prisoner's brother, who is 11 years of age, Inspector Hollingworth said he apprehended the prisoner, who stated that his younger brother gave him the articles in Halton- road, hat lug previously told Han that when he met him he was going to Mr. Imison's to pawn them.—The yourfger brother said the prisoner was not speaking the truth.— Prisoner, who denied his guilt, and told the same story as he had related to the inspector, elected to be summarily dealt with, and was sentenced to receive six strokes with a birch rod.

CHURCH WORK IN WIDNES PARISH. We extract the following twin the Liverpool Parish Messenger :---"The confirmation just over was to Widnes an important event in more respects than one, for while it privileged all to hearthe Lord Bishop of the diocese officiat- ing in our own church for the first time, the service itself was the first confirmation held in the pariah. Hitherto the confirmees have been called upon to go to other churches, as last year, when 74 went from this place to Farnworth Par- ish Church. It was also, to a certain extent, unique, for all the candidates belorezed to our own parish; none were pre- sented by the adjacent parishes. Thus it not only took place in Widnes, but proved to be for Widnes only. The number of names was about three score and ten. rAnd their modesty, reverence, devoutness, and attention, caused even many who had never before seen them, to hope for them the best gifts. May they hold fast so good a confession! They were not all just entering the !settle of life—seine had already long been engaged in the Christian conflict. Not a few are among our most valued Sunday school teachers, and, as such, set a worthy example to many who; still un- confirmed, think lightly, or affect to think lightly, of the laying on of hands. The Church Council has, during the last twelve months, consisted of the churchwardens, sides- men, lay representatives, and honorary organist. The fol- lowing names have been added to this council, for year expiring Easter, 1882. They are men who can work, and we feel sure will bring clear heads, ready hands, and loyal hearts ungrudgingly to the cause of our Church :—Messrs. F. Neil, James Williams, W. Lowe, T. Atherton, Thomas Davies, James Parr, Turton, Dwerryhouse, Whittle, and Crabtree.—Entertainmenm This series closed on May 10th for the present season. The successful carrying through of these entertainments reflects great credit upon all concerned, but particularly upon the ottniser, Mr. J. B. Imisom ; for we cannot forget that it was confidently stated, six months ago, that such entertainments could never succeed in Widnes. The gain has been threefold. First, theZproviding of good healthy amusement during the winter session. Amusement which never raises , the blush or offends the ear;' amusement which called forth abundant of merriment and laughter, pure and spirit-cheering, amusement which introduces to many among us for the first time, standard pieces of song, verse, and humour. Second gain, it has developed the capacity of our glee class, and placed a tangible value upon their volun- tary efforts; 'another such season, and the Widnes Parish Church Glee Class will be a rising power in the locality. It has also revealed to us many outside friends, whose readi- ness to help has been equalled by their faculty to do so. Third gain, we have netted £25, the first stone in our class- room fund, and also nearly ten pounds more towards paying for the piano. But don't let ne forget that £25 might just as easily have been £5O had the congregation more generally come to our help. Some came always, many came never. ' Temperance.—The adult branch of the Church of England Temperance Society has now been fairly commenced. The Vice-Presidents are—Rev. W. H. Duggan, and Messrs. KB- cross and Balmer. The committee is not vet elected; that may be done when we find the most capable men. I think we are fortunate iii securing for the secretary Mr. W. Chad- wick, and for assistant secretary Mr.Farrant. The meetings are weekly, at Waterloo-road schools, at 7-45, a few minute, I after the close of the juvenile meeting, which is held in the sense place, and begins at 6-30. We went not far wrong in , feeling that a temperance society would be uphill work in Widnes—too many wrecks of precious attempts lay scattered I over the past to point even the most sanguine to any other conclusion. This meant and means caution in the framing of the barque, which shall, under God's hlesSing, never founder or strike. As yet our number is small—only 24 in the adult branch, all told. But this cannot long be the case. We must be true to ourselves; every one of us, old or young. ought to belong to one section or the ether of this society, except indeed those who profess to be unable or unwilling, to govern their appetites. When every church officer has enrolled, when each Sunday school teacher has placed his or her name on the list—when the members of our working men's Bible class, and of the young men's Bible class, have basted to common union for common effort—when our pure, noble, and tender-hearted women have stretched out a hand to their weaker sisters, to rescue and encourage—then may we be proud of our society, but hardly until then. Watch, pray, and work.

Mr. DARBY/MIRE moved that the recommendations of the clerk be adopted. Mr. Guatom seconded the motion, which was carried. THE HEALTH OE THE CHILDREN. The DOcrou reported that the general- health of the children was very good. As usual at this time of the year they were very prone to skin diseases. Eczema had appeared in two or three fresh cases. Gymnastic exercises should be provided both for the boys and girls on the Kindergarten system. It was resolved that in accordance with the recommenda- tion of the medical officer, the gymnasium now at the workhouse be transferred to the barracks for the use of the children during the hours of recreation. . .
The minutes—were confirmed. THE STATE OF THE HOUSE.

The MASTER reorted that the number of inmates in the house during last week was 488 against 469 in the cor- responding week of last year. Number of vagrants relieved during the week was :—Men 183, women 30, children 15, total 228. The number of imbeciles or idiots in the work- house are 40. The master and matron on behalf of the sick, thanked the Rev. B. B. Prescott and those kind ladies and gentlemen who accompanied him in their visit to the hos- pital. They brought a number of children along, each child carrying a boquet, and as they went through the several sick wards the children sang with mach feeling and effect that appropriate piece " Here, Lord, we offer Thee all that is fairest." Then each child presented the patients with a boquet, which, in many cases, was very touching. Altogether the scene was impressive, and one not soon to be forgotten. • This conclded the business.
