div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, Jun 18, isk.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, Jun 18, isk.
WIDNES POLICE COURT.

MoNDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook (hakell,Juan THE WARRINGTON GENERAL DRAT ER AND Tits Wmovr. —Sarah Thornton, a married woman of Church-street, who on the Wednesday had bet-tt2ffischarget after having been placed in the dock, in company with another prisoner, on a charge of stealine ten sovereigns from the person of Mr. Wm. Plinston, general dealer, Warrington, was brought up after having been remanded for being druuk and in- capable—The Inspector of Police said that the magistrate would recollect the circumstances under which the prisoner was sOt at liberty on the previous Wednesday, and since that time she had been taken up for being drunk and incapable. When apprehended a considerable sum of money was found upon her, and he believed that he should be able to bring some new evidence before the Bench, which joined to the fact of the money being found upon her, would justify them in committing her for trial.—P.C. Pitt said he apprehended the prisoner in Waterloo-road, in a drunken and incapable state and in her satchel the sum of £4 13s. 31d. was found. The money, which was wrapped in a piece of rag, was much discoloured, as though it had leen hidden away. On the 2nd instant, he took the prisoner in custody upon a charge of stealing £lO from the broker Plinston, but though she was carefully examined by the female searcher, no money was found upon her. He and another officer were engaged two days in searching Thornton's house, with the object of discovering the cash, but with no success:—ln defence, the woman stated that the money found upon her was her own, and part of the sum of £33 left her by an aunt, on the 6th March last. It had never been out of her possession since she received it.—The Inspector remarked that the prisoner had been spending money freely since her discharge on Wednesday, and it was somewhat singular that the same expended and what was found upon her, amounted to about the stolen £lo.—Prisoner was remanded until

Wednesday. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. H. S. Hall (chairman) Mr. Holkrook Gaskell senr., and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell junr. A FEROCIOUS Doc ORDERED TO BE DESTROYED.—SamueI Barrow, labourer, was summoned by a boy named William O'Foole, for allowing a ferocious dog to be at large, on the 9th inst. From the evidence of complainant and Mr. Shepherd, market inspector to the Widnes Local Board, it appeared that the lad was going up Waterloo-road, at about eight o'clock at. night, when without any provocation, the defendant's retriever dog set upon him and bit him on the hand and behind. Complainant had suffered considerable pain since and been unable to sleep properly. He also sa w the animal attack a woman and take a piece oat of her shawl. A man named Clarke, who happened to be in court, was called, and said the dog had attacked him three times, and he felt sure that but for the interference of the woman with whom de- fendant lodged, he would have been severely bitten. Mrs. Millington, defendant's landlady, said he had had the dog four years. She described the attack of the animal upon the last witness as merely his play." (Laughter.) The Chairman said it was not fair to the public that a dog of such a character as that possessed by the defendant should go at large; and the magistrates ordered that it must be destroyed in the presence of the Inspector of Police. Defen- dant would also have the costs to pay. A BAD Frsn CASE.—AN AMUSING DEFENDANT.—SamueI John Francis, fish dealer, was summoned by Mr. John Dickson, Inspector of Nuisances to the Widnes Local Board, under the Food and Drugs Act, for exposing a number of periwinkles and apples for sale, which were unfit for food. Mr. Beasley appeared on behalf of the Local Board, and seid that on the previous Wednesday the defeedant's shop was visited by Mr. Dickson and Mr. Shepherd, the Market Hall Inspector. In the window they found a number of peri- winkles and apples which were quite unfit for food. There were 2,072 periwinkles and the defendant was suremoned under the 116 and 117 sections of the Public Health Act, by which a certain penalty was fixed for each piece of fish exposed; and if the full penalty was inflicted in the case he would have to pay £43,463. (Laughter.) There were 48 apples. The periwinkles and apples were bought from defendant by a lad named Samuel Millington. The stock of periwinkles and apples were seized, and submitted to Mr. Brock, J.P., who ordered them to be destroYed.—Evidence, in support of the case was given by Mr. Dickson, Mr. Shep- herd, Samuel Millington (a lad), and John Massey.—De- fendant caused much amusement in court by the manner in which he cross-examined the witnesses, whichh edidat great length. He produced two specimens of periwinkles in court, and said that the live one was exactly similar to those which had bees seized. He then, very gravely, pulled the fish out of its shell, and said he should like any gentle- man in court to taste it for the purpose of saying whether he thought it good or not. As none of the gentlemen round the solicitors' table—not even the Inspector of Police— offered to swallow the periwinkle, he did so himself, amidst the laughter of the spectators. He graphically described the largeness of his family, and the indefatigable efforts which be had put forth to supply the public of Widneswith an honest article of food. But he, like many a well-mean- ing man, had at times been foiled in his efforts—in hie case by the weather. At the conclusion of his address, com- pared with which that of Mr. Beasley was a mere nothing, he set down, with a self-complacent look, at the solicitors' table. A. policeman, who was evidently astonished at defendant's coolness, went up to him and requested that he would move and take his place, at what we may by courtesy call the bar. This he did, and when the paper bag had been handed to him containing his specimens of shell fish, and he had put it in his pocket, he appeared happy once more —The Chairman stated that it was fortunate for the defendant that the Local Board bad stated they did not with to press the case, and he would only be tined 20s. and 15e, colts in the case of thp periwinkles. The summons as to the apples would be dismissed. CRUELTY TO A HORSE BY A Sr. HELENS MAN.—An old man, named William Bradley, a carrier, living at St. Helens, was charged with being guilty of cruelty to a horse, by :Mowing it to be worked on the let jest., and Thomas Bradley with working it.—?. C. Strickland said that about three o'clock in the aPernoon, he saw the defendant's horse drawing a tarry in Bedford-street, Lugsdale. Under the animal's collar was a wOund about the size of half-a-crown, from which matter was running slightly. On the side of one shoulder were some smaller wounds' and a rather large one on the top of the chine. Underneath the saddle was a wound from which matter was oozing, and another one full of matter. He drew the attention of the driver to the fact, and he took the horse out of the lurry.—P. C. Montgomery gave corroborative evidence —The old man denied the charge, and said the horse was a very good one and sold to him by Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., who favoured him in the purchase, owing to his being one of his old servants. He called his eon's wife, who denied that there was any wound on the animal when it was taken out.—Mr. Gasket' said the summons against the carter would be dismissed, but the old man would he fined 208.. and costs 78. 6d. MAINTA/NINT; A CHILD IN AN INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL.— On the application of the police, Thomas Burns, who it was proved was in receipt of 28s. 64. wages weekly, was ordered to contribute 31. per week towards the support of his two children, who are in Beacon-lane Industrial School, Liver- pool. The ease was proved by the luspector and P. C. Clarkson. A DISHONEST PARTNER.—THE DRINE AGAlN.—Joseph Hughes, bricklayer, was brought up on remand, charged with stealing £4 10s., the money of Michael Duggan and three other men. The evidence showed that Hughes and some fellow-workmen, including 'the prosecutor, entered Into a kind of partnership to do a certain sort of rough work at Messrs. Hutchineon'A chemical works, and divide the ninney they earned. On the 4th instant £4 was due to the men, and the prisoner drew it and Apent it in drink. Prisoner afterwerds gave himself up, to the Garston police. There apneeredillbe a difficulty in dealing with the case as a pure felony, owing to the quaei-partnership existing be- tween Hughes, the preesecnter, and his fellow wentmen, and Mr. Gasketl said it would be better for the poor men if the prisoner would agree to pay the money.—Mr. Rigby, as- sistant overseer, who was in court on other business, was called by the prisoner. and said he had known him for about 12 months as a straightforward, honest man, and he did not believe he had any felonious intention in what he had done.—After Mr. John Reyes. pay clerk at Messrs. Hutch- inson'e, had also given the prisoner a good character, he was discharged on promising to repay the money to the men. THE WARRINGTON BROKER, AND HIS ADVENTURE WITH THE WIDOW. Sarah Thornton, a respectably-dressed woman, of Chnrch-street, wee brought up. having been remanded on Monday, upon a charge of being drunk, and was now charged, in conjunction with her sister, Catherine Gordon, a marrbal woman, with stealing £lO from the person of Mr. William Plinston, grocer, Catherine-street, Warring- ton, on the Ist inst., under circumstances which have been fully reported in The Examiner. The prosecutor gave evidence as on the previous occasion when the prisoners were charged with the theft, as did also P.C. Pitt.—James B. Hunt, Church-street, spoke to redeeming a number of articles of clothing for the prisoner Thornton, after she was liberated on the Bth inst. On the first occasion she gave him 295., on the second £l., en the third 18s., and on the fourth 35., for the purpose of doing so.—James Leigh, bar- man at the Sian Inn, said that on the evening of the Bth Inst., the two prisoners and a man called at the public:house and hid some whiskey and beer, for which Thornton paid. She tendered him a half-a-crown in payment, but as it was a bad one he gave it her back. She then said she had plenty of money, and gave him a sovereign, out of which he took payment.—Frederick Winstanley, biil if, Oakland- street, said that on the 24th ult., he distrained on the prisoner Thornton's goods for £l, which was due for rent She endea- voured to raise the money, but as she did not succeed he seized a nnmber of articles of furniture, which he had still in his possession.—Robert Foley, chemical works labourer, spoke to being in the house when Plinston was there, and to his (Plinston) going out and Afterwards returning with an officer to claim the money he bad lost.—Mary Sullivan, the searcher employed at the police station, said she searched the prisoners when they were taken into custody on the evening of the Ist-inst. She found no money on Thornton, but on Gordon Is. 7d. and a key.—Thornton now adhered to the stBtement she made on Monday, to the effect that the money found in her possession was part of £33 left her by her mother, in last March. Gordon said she knew nothing tf eedeeeeir, and added that she was aware her sister had had money left.--Prisoners were committed for trial at the Liverpool Sessions, which commence en the 12th prox. d2n ee damages. WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Mr. Jos. Harrison, chairman, presided at the forfal7 meeting of -tltis Board; held---at-tterWorkhouse -on Wedrtes, day. There were also present the Revs. B. B. Prescott, E. C. E. Carleton, and G. F. Roberts, Major Cartwright, and Messrs. Derbyshire, Ha". Jeans, Woolfall, Woods, Kilshall, Mackie, Hunt, Fairhur: riarnett, Swinton, Greene% Black- burst, Humphreys, and per. Mr. MACKIE made 'some observations as to the increase in salaries made at tne last meeting of the Board, but the Chairman ruled him out of order. THE SUPPLY OF SPIRITS.

The CLERIC read the following letter, dated 2nd June, which he had received from Messrs. Rowson and Son:— Dear sir,—ln reply to your note dated June Ist, the whisky we have supplied to the Union Workhouse at 15s 6d per gallon is old whisky, and a spirit we never had a complaint of ; and we feel sure the Guardions themselves have not sampled it. We tendered at the above price, thinking it would be high enough. If the finest quality is wanted we shall be happy to supply, and will send samples if required and price list. We may add that whisky varies in price from 14s to 28s per gallon. The CLERK remarked that the matter was disposed of at the last meeting.

THE WORKHOUSE RAND IN REQUEST. The following applications for the services of the Work- house band were considered :—" We should consider it a favour if you could allow your band to enliven our children's annual school treat, as you have kindly done for some years past. The treat will be held as usual in the schoolroom, Vitrol-square, on Wednesday, the 22nd inst., at 2-30 p.m.—Yours faithfully, Wm. SIMPSON, Sankey Sugar Works, Earlestown."—" We are giving our friends and customers a free trip to Southport on Monday, the 27th Inst., and we shall be pleased if the whole of the members of the Board and their wives will honour us with their Com- pany on that occasion. The distance being so abort, South- port is reached before a thought of fatigue suggests itself to the traveller.—Trusting you will accept our invitation, we are, yours respectfully, JESPER, KITCHING and Co." The CHAIRMAN said Messrs. Jesper, Kitchiug and Co. had made an application for the band, which the Barracks Committee recommended should be acceded to. Mr. GARNETT : Have you received an invitation from the Grand Clothing Hall Company? (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN: No; but I quite expect one when they hear what their enterprising neighbours have done. Mr. HALL moved that the band be permitted to go to Earlestown. It would be a treat for the children, who would no doubt be well looked after. Mr. WOOLFALL observed that Friday was Walking Day, the Wednesday following the band was wanted at Eatles- town, and on Monday, the 27th, there was an application for it to go to Southport; and in a month there would be the annual workhonse trip. He wished to know where they would draw the line, as the children would be out too often. Major CARTWRIGHT inquired if the children received'any 1 remuneration. The CHAIRMAN said there was generally a , collection made, and sometimes a considerable stlin of money was obtained. There was no specific sum named. Major CARTWRIGHT remarked that if this thing was allowed to go on the children would be away one half of their time. (Hear, bear.) . Mr. DAR/11'511MM seconded the motion, which was cart led. The application of Mears. Jesper, Kitching, and Co., for the services of the band had been considered by the Barracks Committee, and recommended for approval; and at a later period of the sitting the request was granted. It was under- stood that any., member of the Board who wished to avail himself of their invitation could do se. THE SUPPLY OE STATIONERY. Before the passing of the accounts, Mr. Gator= observed that there was an account from Mr. George Powl- son of £l4 lie. Scl. for school requisites, which he thought might have been got cheaper. There was an item of £5 for school desks, and he should like to know if there was an ,estimate for those articles. The CLERK did not think there was. Major CARTWRIGHT said the atatienery account was a very small one—between £2OO and £3OO. He had seen a bill that the House Committee had ordered from another piece, and it was written across, "All orders for statione, y must be ordered by the clerk." He thought it very strange that the committee could not give an order and send it to whom they thought proper. He had been told by a person upon whose word he could rely, thal the trade discount was from.2s per cent to 35 per cent, but he had not seen a bill there upon which more than five per cent had been allowed, and that only in one instance. When the trade got 25 per cent to 35 per cent, he thought they ought to have some little advantage at all events, so long as they were under contract for the whole of their supply. Mr. GARNETT said he noticed that 63. was charged for two dozen copy books. He doubted whether any gentle- man connected with a school ever paid more than 3d. The CLERK said that for many years the Board purchased their books from the London stationers, who, having a monopoly would not depart from their usual costs, and it transpired that if the contractor for the year could buy these booke, he would have a discount from the London publishers that they would not allow the Union. It was understood that if the contractor would not exceed the charges of the London publishers he should have the pri- vilege of obtaining the books. With reference to the orders for stationery; the bills passed through his hands, so that they might go direct to the right quarter, and that he should be able to see that due economy was exercised in their pur- chase, and that there might be uniformity in the accounts. This would not interfere with the directions of the com- mittee. The CHAIRMAN : I suppose you get discount of 5 per cent, off the orders sent to London Major CART'WTIIGHT : No, no; only in one case. A Member remarked that discount was only allowed on printed books. Major CARTWRIGHT Well, we are told that an allowance of 25 per cent. is made. The CLERK : I don't know anything about that. I should not think so. Major CARTWRIGHT : I have it from one who is in the trade. The CHAIRMAN : Do you mean to say that if we gave all our orders to a London firm we should get a discount of 25 per cent, in the stationery department ? Major CARTWRIGHT said a stationer could get supplied mm the London houses at a discount of 25 per mint., and if a local tradesman was satisfied with a profit of Ifj per cent., and could save the Board 15 per cent, by the transaction, he ought to have it. Mr. HALL did not think they need discuss this matter. It mizht ha correct what Major Cartwright stated, that they could put this 25 per cent, in competition in Warrington and other townships, but he did not think any stationer would take leas or that the Union could get any per cent. It was a question whether they would give the contractor the privilege of supplying London books. They knew what lie got out of it. Mr. BrAextruasT said the London firms wonldnot give the union the privileges that they did to the trade, and as they could not gain anything by sending to London,. they ought to give the local tradesman the privilege of supplying the books. Mr. Harm thought the Board had a considerable saving even at the price they paid for their stationery, but if they wanted to put this 25 per cent, in the market they must ask every stationer in the town to tender. One might be satistledwith 10 per cent, and another 15 per cent., which of course would reduce the Board's percentage con- siderably. The Crum remarked that the Board should understand that there was a contract, and the profits with which the contractor would be satisfied was clearly a matter for his own consideration. Mr. ISfacxrE said as the clerk had expressed it, it Was under- etood that all books requited by the union that were neces- sarily manufactured in London, should come from the local contractor, and on the faith of that he tendered for his own printing at a remarkably low price. With reference to the supplying of the school desks, no doubt the committee instead of sending and getting them from the present contractor, got them from Mr. Powlson, , who was possibly the agent for Mr. Heywood, the famed supplier of these goods, but it would have been better if the committee had followed the nasal course of sending to the current contractor, taking care that he never got more than 10s. per cent, upon anything he supplied from a distance. If inquiry were made Mr. Powlson would, be found to have charged a reasonable price, but at the same time he was not the right man to be sent to. Mr. GARNETT moved that the accounts be passed. The two dozen copy books he had spoken of might mean six dozen as the bill mentioned three kinds, and that would make A considerable reduction in the price. The CHAIRMAN said the present contract exists until next April, and it would be useless to prolong the discussion. At that time it would be competent for any member to propose a modification of the present arrangement. Mr. WOODS seconded the passing of the accounts, which was carried. RE-APPOINTMENT OF A SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICER. Mr. COOPER moved that Mr. Hobson, school attendance officer for Penketh district, be re-appointed at a salary, of £75 as heretofore. , rite resolution was seconded, and carried unanimously. THE SALE OF INTOXICATING DRINK ON SUNDAYS. The CLERK read a petition against the sale of intoxicat- ing liquors on Sundays, which he had received from the Central Association for stopping the sale of intoxicating liquors on Sunday. Mr. DARBYSHIRE moved that the petition be passed. Every member knew from experience that the drinking customs of this country were the cause of a great deal of the pauperisn with which they had to contend in that work- house. (Hear, hear.) If there .was one day on which a man should abstain from drinking it was on the Sabbath, and he had therefore great pleasure in proposing that the Board sign the petition. A number of towns had been canvassed to ascertain whether the inhabitants were in favour of closing of public houses on a Sunday, and iths of the inhabitants of these towns were in favour of that step. Mr. MACKIE seconded the motion. He was in favour of the measure and wished that it extended, not merely to the present public houses, but also to clubrooms. (Hear, hear.) He belonged to two clubs in London [Major CARTWDIGT, sarcastically: The Reform Club.]i—t is the Reformed Club —and he could get anything he liked at any hour. The

publicans would largely agree to any arrangement of this kind if it was made compulsory. The Rev. E. C. E. CoarroN supported the resolution, and said he should have liked to have seen embodied in the peti- tion a proposal for.the_cloSing of public houses on the dart of polling in Parliamentary elections. Mr. GARNETT supported the motion, remarking that if they got the public houses closed, clubs would be bound to follow. Major CARTWRIGHT thought it a step in the right direct- tion. When Mr. Mackie concluded his speech on clubs he looked direct,st him. [Mr. MACKIE : That's a mistake.] He did. (Laughter.) Major Cartwright could assure Mr. Mr. Mackie that he was not a member of any club, but whilst in favour of closing public houses he thought they might leave out clubs. He remarked that a partial closing of public houses would do no good, and said Sir Andrew Walker closed his houses in Warrington on a Sunday. Mr. DA/unman: Closed at the front and open at the back. (Laughter.) - Mr. WOODS said the one in Mersey-street was open. Mr. GARNETT: That is kept open for you, perhaps. Mr. HUMPHREYS said Sunday drinking of late had de- creased, and, in his opinion, th.re would be more Sunday drunkenness if the houses were closed. (Hear, hear.) They would take it home on a Saturday night without any judgment, and as it was they were kept within bounds. Mr. WINSTANLEY : If they take it home on the Saturday night they will drink it on the Saturday night. (Laughter.) Mr. COOPER thought it would be best to let those mem- bers sign the petition who wished to do so. Mr. WLITSTANLEY would be glad to see the measure car- ried, as it would be a hardship to none and a great boon to the public. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN said: Before putting this to the vote I should like to say a few words upon the subject, although I den'ttbink they will be in harmony with the opinions that have been already expressed, still they are my opinions, and lam not afraid to utter them. lam as desirous as anyone that Sunday drunkenness should cease, but I don't think closing public houses would accomplish it. I think it would be better to let the matter alone legislatively, and trust to the moral sense, religious feeling, decorum, and propriety of our countrymen. Drunkenness has already ceased to exist as a prevalent vice among the higher classes of the country.—(Mr. Garnett: No, no.)—As a prevalent vice I say among the higher classes. But it has assuredly not been by any direct operation of the law that this happy revolution has been brought about. It is far better, and likely to be more lasting, that men should learn to reisist temptation, than that they should be shielded from It bY a law in I opposition to their OWD wishes. (Hear, hear.) The working classes are still, no doubt, too much addicted to drunkenness—(hear, hear)—not because they have greater opportunities for it than their richer neighbours, but simply because they have greater temptations and weaker connterbalancing tastes. Then again, all law to be operative, should he an embodiment of common assent, it should also (to be just) be impartial in its applica- tion; but a law which prevents a poor man from procuring a pint of ale from the public-house for his Sunday's dinner, but which does not prevent a rich man from procuring a bottle of wine at his club or from his own cellar; is decidedly not impartial is its application. (Hear, hear.) The tap of the rich man, from the necessity of his wealth, is in his dwn cellar. The tap cf the poor man, from the necessity ofjais poverty, is in the cellar of the publican. If we are to hive legislation upon this subject let it be so that it may affect rich and poor alike. To close public-houses on a Sunday would, in my opinion, only increase the very evil which the doting of them Is intended to remely. (Hear, hear.) So long as people will have drink, it is better they should have It in a well regulated houSe, which is open to supervision, than in private houses, amongst women and children, with all its unwholesome surroundings, and where people could get drunk with impunity. Under present circumstances, a publidan would imperil his license, if he were to serve a drunken man with drink, or permit drunkenness in his house, but. in private-houses or cottages, no one has a right to interfere, and the closing of public,houses on a Sunday, while it would inflict great inconvenience upon many peaceable inhabitants in both 'town and country, would answer no good or useful end. (Hear, hear). On the motion being put, 14 voted for the petition and 7 against.

..... VOTE OP cONDOLENCE. The Barracks Committee's minute& contained the follow- ing letter of condolence addressed to Mr. Longshaw : —lndustrial Schools, Wilson-Patten street, Warrington, 7th June, 1881.—Dear Sir.—We, the undersigned, members of the committee, officers, and servants of the above schools, desire to express to you our sincere sorrow for the melan- choly accident which has recently befallen your dear son William. We feel that the pleasant.nature of your inter- course and association with this institution daring the past year, as a member of our committee, renders our earnest sympathies the more imperative; and, while we are fully I mindful of the extretne pain so sadden a calamity must have caused you, and the other members of your family, we pray God, in His infinite mercy, may comfort you all in your bereavement and distress.—Signed John Yonge, George Appleton, Joseph Harrison, E. Blackurst; E. C. E. Carleton, W. E. Winstanley, John Greenall, Thomas Hunt. -

div.head: WORICHOESE SCHOOL EXAMINATrON.--TER TEACHERS
div.p: THE WORICHOESE SCHOOL EXAMINATrON.--TER TEACHERS
CONGRATULATED.

Mr. H. M. MINES, the superintendent at the Barracks, re- ported that for the week ending June 7th, there wete 100 boys, 55 girls, and 1$ infants—total 173—attending school. Of this number 40 boys and 40 girls were remising indus- trial training. During the week ending, 14th June 181 children attended school. The following is the result of the school examination held by J. R. Mozley; Esq., Her Majesty's Inspector of Poor Law Schools, on the 27th ult.: Eighty boys and thirty-six girls were presented for exami- nation. Six boys were presented in the sixth standard, and six in the fifth standard, all of whom passed successfully. In the fourth standard ten boys and six girls were presented, and six boys and four girls passed. In the third standard twelve boys and four girls were examined, all of whom passed successfully; and of the sixteen boys and fifteen girls presented in the second standard ten boys and thirteen girls passed. In the first standard thirty boys and eleven girls were presented, and fifteen boys and two girls passed. Of the eighteen boys who passed successfully in the higher standards, twelve are entitled to certificates of proficiency, having passed in every subject, while the four girls who passed in the fourth standard are also entitled to certificates. The percentage of passes in the higher standards is boys 100 per cent, girls 86 per cent.--At a meeting of the com- mittee it wan moved by Mr. HARRISON, seconded by Mr. BLACKIIIIIIST, and carried unanimously, that a vote of con- gratulation be given to the teachers upon the successful result of their labours during the past year. Mr. GARNETT was much pleased with the inspector's report, and believed the children wire being efficiently taught. He adverted to the industrial exhibition in the Co-operative Hall, in connection with the Society of Friends, and the excellency of the work produced by the children' in all the departments, speaking particularly of the joinery and cabinet miring. It gave a lad great power why he was able to handle tools for whatever course of life he was in- tended, and it would be a capital thing if in connection with the Workhouse school they could have some sort of shop-in which instruction might be given. Mr. BLACERVSET said the Barracks Committee had con- sidered the matter, but inasmuch as they were only tempor- arily located at the Barracks, it had been thought best to defer the question until they got settled in the new schools. Major Careewnrearr and Mr. WINSTANLEY concurred that the new schools were built with the express idea of giving the children en industrial training. Mr. COOPER said the master informed him that all those boys who had passed the sixth standard were ready to go out to work, and he hoped the committee would obtain situations for them.

The minutes were confirmed. TIEE FRIENDS' INDUSTRIAI, EXHIBITION. It was resolved that the master take those boys of a com- petent age to see the .Friends' industrial exhibition at the Co-operative Hall, it being understood that it payment was required several members would be willing to bear the charges.

div.head: AcPPOINTMENT OF A._ SUPERINTENDENT.
div.p: AcPPOINTMENT OF A._ SUPERINTENDENT.

The minutes of the House Committee contained a recom- mendation for the temporary appointment of a superinten- dent in place of Samuel Greenway. Major CARTWRIGHT moved the adoption of the minutes, and stated the considerations which had caused the com- mittee ta make the recommendation. Mr. WooLrarm seconded the motion. Mr. WlNgrertuty moved an amendment, that the minutes pass with the exception of that referring to the appointment of an additional assiotant, Mr.BLecxnurtsr. seconded the amendment.
-.— Mr. HEATON said the• assistance was required, and if the Government inspector came down and went through the house there would, be a row, and the Board would be in it.

Mr. MacKutrusr asked the master if he could not manage until next September. The MASTER: it IS an absolute necessity if you wish the ohl people to be looked after. Five members voted for the amendment and 12 against, and the original motion was therefore carried.

div.head: RULES FOR ADMISSION OF SICK PAUPERS.
div.p: RULES FOR ADMISSION OF SICK PAUPERS.

Major Cutvwntartr referred to the temporary orders given for relief in the house, and asked whether, if a sick person wasadmitted to the house, it should not be tempor- arily and with an order of removal. The CLARE : You cannot if he is sick, but he can be re- moved if the sickness is permanent. Major CARTWRIGHT said so long as he was in the house during sickness a week or a fortnight, a man was taken no notice of if he took his discharge; and what he wanted, as chairman of the House Committee, was, that all orders in future, if the applicant did not belong to the Union, should be for removal. The CLERK. said there was a legal difficulty. The law said, not that a person could not be removed because of his sickness, but that a person could not be removed if sickness caused the chargeability. Major CATWRIGHT : Then you may put him on a sus- pension order. The CLERIC: You cannot do it unless it is a permanent sickness. He suggested that printed regulations should be posted throughout the house, that orders for admission of paupers are granted upon the follow- ing basis :—That in the case of a pregnant woman, mother and child shall be brought before the House, Com- mittee one month after confinement, if in a fit state to appear. and tliat the inshuctions of the committee shall be taken with regard to her. That persons adrnitt4l to the house be- cause they are sick shall apply to the Board for re-admission when convalescent. These, the clerk remarked, Would settle the whole thing, because as it was they were never brought up at all.

It will not bear thePebrulagthhtenesdescoafy;he delay." u.s of its history and uses:— " 'Twas here the buzz of eager nations ran, In murmured pity or loud roared applause, As man was slaughtered by his fellow-man." 4, ‘ * a " Butchered to make a Roman holiday." a a * * * " But here, where murder breathed her bloody stream : And here, where buzzing nations choked the ways, And roared or murmured like a mountain stream, Dashing or wa idering as the tarred strays; Here, where the Roman millions praise or blame, Was life or death; the play-thug of a crowd! My voice sounds much; and fall the stars' faint rays On the arena void, seats crushed, walls bowed, And galleries, whey my steps seem echoes, strangely loud." Thankful indeed should we be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ that such places have now the silence of death reigning over them! and that the Gospel of His Son has elevated even the tastes and amusements of nations to a level so much higher than Paganism, or even Popery with her bell fights, as in Spain, could ever attain to. This vast amphitheatre was commenced two years after the destruction of Jerusalem, and probably completed in twelve or fifteen years. It seated 87,000 people, and had standing room for 13,000 more. It was the great centre of Roman entertainments. Within its walls, during the whole' of an appointed summer's day, the emperors and the Roman People, from the highest to the lowest, were wont to revell in the savage delight of seeing men fight to death with wild, beasts, and also with their fellow men. Sometimes on thel broad arena scattered with sand the gladiators met in mortal conflict ; and then, in order to vary the amusement, and to increase the excitement and bloodshed, naval fights would' take place on the lake beneath the spacious platform, which had to be lifted and removed. Around the bed of this lake, recently excavated, we saw the dens out of which the wild I beasts used to spring through the trap-doors upon their human antagonists. We also observed a second pit belong- ing to each of these dens, in which, probably, a water- balance, or some such appliance, worked, and threw the beasts to the surface of the platform. The grooves for the sheaves, over which the ropes passed, were still there. At the dedication of the building 5,000 wild beasts were destroyed; at what expenses of life history does not shoe ; but the exhibition lasted 100 days, and we may imagine what the slaughter would be. During 500 years the Colosseum was the scene of these infernal sports. Many martyrs perished on it arena during the Persecution of the early Christians, among whom was Ignatius, whe was brought from Antioch to be devoured by the wild beasts. The arch of Titus, which stands not far from the Colosseum, as you come into the city by the Appian way, must not be ever-looked. It is supposed to , commemorate the taking of Jerusalem by Titus. Beneath, its arch are still preserved, in beautiful basreliefe, the I triumphal chariot of the emperor, as he advanced to the ' Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus ; also the ark of the covenant and the seven-branched candlestick, "borne in this triumphal precession as the most precious spoil of the Jewish temple." What a noble relic! Sacred and profane history seam to meet under its lofty archway, and, in their testimony to the truth of Christianity, to send the echo of their united voices right down the ages. The Appian way! With what profound reverence we travelled along, as we found our feet for the first time in the track of Paul, the great Apostle of the Gentiles! It was along this very road the Roman brethren went forth to meet the aged Christian veteran, as he drew nigh to Rome, after his long and perilous journey from Cesarea and conducted him into the city, with his heart bounding with gratitude to God, and his soul inspired with fresh courage by their brotherly greeting; though the image of the detestable Nero must have risen before him. Paul, like a brave citizen and Christian hero, had thrown himself upon his country's laws, as a "power ordained of God." Ile had made his appeal from a provincial tribunal to Caesar's judgment-seat, and now went calmly for- ward to meet the result. Within the palace of the Cresars, on the Palatine Hill, we stood in the very Hall of Justice, and, if so, on the very spot where Paul was arraigned and made his defence before Nero; on which occasion we read, "no man stood by him, but all forsook him." Among the various deeply interesting remains which the recent excava- tions have brought to light on the Palatine Hill, none can excite a deeper feeling in the heart of the Christian than this noble ruin—the "Basilica Jot-is." Within this spacious hall, whose windows must have commanded a view of the whole city, it is quite certain justice was administered by the reigning emperor in early Christian times. The broken remains of the marble seat in which the emperor sat is still visible, and also a beauti- ful remnant of the teibune-rail. Perhaps more interesting still is a circular marble slab worked into the Mosaic pave- ment about 40 feet from the rail, and right in the middle of the hall. On this slab, about 44 inches in diameter, stood the prisoner guarded by Roman soldiers, while a passage was kept clear betweer him and his imperial judge. On that very stone Paul must have stood menacled hand and foot,—Paul! the noblest of Roman citizens, and the most illustrious of all Christian heroes stood there in chains and before—Nero. The remains of several temples and palaces, built or extended by the various emperors, Nero amongst the number, have been opened on the Palatinellill. On some of the walls inscriptions of the deepest interest have been discovered. One in particular was pointed out by our guide, in looking at which you almost feel time obliterated, and arif the jeers and laughter of the scoffing crew around it were sounding in 'your ears. It is a caricature of the crucifixion on the wall of the guard house, evidently sketched by a Roman soldier or servant in the apostolic age. The crucified One is drawn with a donkey's head; a scur- rilous rem irk underneath the figure indubitably fixing it upon Jesus of Nazareth. While such things in themselves shock the feelings, what strong foundations they lay beneath the feet of the Christian as testimonies to the reality and truth of the religion of Christ. Before tearing ourselves away from this entrancing regkre in which cluster wfthin the compass of a few acres so many maenificent relics of Rome's past greatness, and over which' is shed in such lustrous streaks the reflex glory of early Christian times, let us descend from the Palatine into the Forum, or the great square in which all the public business of ancient Rome was conducted. Covered up during the reign of the Popes with rubbish of all kinds it is now in courts of excavation, and will soon be laid bare in every part. The excavations, car- ried on from day to day, excite a great amount of interest \ in the public mind. Seldom is the Forum without a crowd of people watching the workmen as they turn over the soil; always eager for some new discovery. In Rome's palmiest days "thirty-one great roads centred in the caßital, which, issuing out of the Forum, traversed Italy, ran through the provinces, and were terminated only-by the boundary of her empire." As a starting point a gilt pillar was set up by Augustus, in the middle of the Forum, upon which was written the distances to the various places. This pillar was discovered in 1823. In this grand area there stands disclosed the remains of several monuments, temples, altars, porticos, dm., at which sacrifices were offered to the gods, from which orators of Rome addressed the people, and before which the bodies of the departed heroes, as in the case of• Julius Coml., were burned—a mark of the highest posthumous honour that could be paid by a grateful people. To travel along the roadway leading into the square almost makes one hold his breath! The heavy boulder, pavement has recently been uncovered, and presents to view the deep ruts made by chariot wheels, which it must have required years and years of wear and tear to scoop out. Fervid and fierce, indeed, must have been the everyday life of Rome to account for such marks of it upon her thoroughfares. Along this road, and up to the temple of Saturn, the victorioue generals had to go in procession, to make oath that they had given a correct account of their priconers and spoils. This same road formed part of the sacred way which ran from the Colosseum to the Capitol, and up which the returning con- querors always advanced that they might receive the plaudits of the people, and the victor's crown. As you enter this once fine square, along the sacred way, you have on the left the ruins of the temple of Castor and Pollux, three splendid pillars of which are still standing. I refer to this especially, because I wish to show, by an anecdote con- nected with it, how much the minds of both rulers and people in that iron are were sometimes led away by trifles. It is recorded by Pliny that a raven was hatched upon the roof of this temple, and, as a fledgeling, made its home in a bootmaker's shop opposite. Instructed, pro- bably, by the hootmaker, it used to fly every morning to the Rostra facing the Forum, where it would salute the Emperor Tiberius Germanicus, and others as they passed with some weed of compliment. This it did for several years, till a jealous neighbour of the bootnnaker killed RA For this the man was put to death, while the bird was honoured with a public funeral. It is said that no emperor or distinguished citizen of Rome had ever such a burial, the concourse of people was so great and the obsequies so grand. To the right of this temple, and about the centre of the Forum, stands an ob- ject of surprising in terest—Ctesar's Rostra, the base of which is still extant. Near to this Rostra. which stands to one side of the "Via Sacra," as it approaches the Capitol, it is pro- bable Ctesar's body was burned, after Mark Antony had delivered his famous oration over it. From this place, also, it is supposed, Cicero hurled his Philippi cs against Malt Antony ; and in turn had his own head and hands hung upon it, after Mark Antony, haying compassed his death, and re- ceived them with laughter and exultation, had satiated him- self with the sight. What a picture of public life in ancient times! When we compare it with the amenities of public life in our own country and times,how much we should feel our indebtedness to the religion of Jesus Christ for the wonder- ful change. To nothing else than to its benign spirit can be traced so blessed an amelioration of the social state. For the opportunity of seeing all these, and many other remains of ancient Rome, we are indebted to the energy and public spirit of Victor Emmanuel and his government, whose care to preserve the developed trreasnres of antiquity is as great as their researches are persevering. One of our party had rather an uncomfortable proof of this official vigilance. In passing through one of the disburied rooms of the Palatine, he had been seen, probably by a rival guide to ours, to pick up a bit of tesselated pavement, about half an inch square, from the floor. We had not proceeded far when one of the liveried guards came up, and breathlessly inquired who had broken the pavement. Our frisnd said he had pot broken off, but simply lifted up, a single bit. Still

he had to follow the exer to the entrance gate, and to give his Do:me and address. Communications followed him to I)amascus, our highly respectable guide in Rome havi_sg had his certificate meanwhile suspended; and tho matter was not finally arranged until our friend re- turned to Europe, and forwarded the costs, some twenty or \ thirty shillings to Rome. I must now bring my account of Rome to a close. I could say much more. I haveTr9.l.- ing about the baths of Caracalla—those wonderful ruins; nor of the Catacombs, more wonderful still • nor of the Panthecn, "Shrine of all saints, and temple of all gods, from Jove to Jesus—spared and blessed by times." But lam ' sttisfied, if, in passing through the faded glories of the present,—and the ghostly shadows of the past, I have pre- s nted enough to deepen the assurance that God is ever pre- sent in history, and that He has set bounds over which no- thin z has been allowed to pass. In contemplating the fate of pagan Rome in her disinterred remains, we do well to re- member how rapid and irretrievable was her ruin,—that it was from the pinnacle of pride and power that she, becoming a persecutor of the Church of God, fell by steps the most signal and disasterous, until, being prostrated by the over- flowinl, wars and paralysing decrees of Constantine, she was literally buried alive by barbarian hordes, who, in the recoil of her wicked prosecutions, had come from dark unknown forests to avenge those who, driven from Rome, had carried the story of the cross among their savage tribes. Not with- out reason, says Dr. Kip, did Alaric the Visigoth style him- self "The Scourge of God ;" and when he led his fiery countrymen over the Alps, and made his name a watchword of terror, he was fulfilling his mission as fully as Cyrus, when God sent bins forth in defence and for the restoration of his ancient people—the Jews. (To be continued next iteek.)

Defendant was fined is. and

Row- bottom on Saturday night, and being drunk and disorderly, Patrick Mellor was fined 10s. and costs. BY A SOUTR-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. [SrsotAx..] no. 111. ONWARD TO ROME. Our progress from Turin to Rome was by easy stages, irst to Florence then to Rome, The advent of Victor Emmanuel, by which the imperial city was constituted the capital and political centre of an united Italy, is to be re- garded as one of the greatest facts of modern history. The liberation of a noble and intelligent people from the rule of Use pope, the lawless barbarities of a Bomba, and the im- potent and degrading tyrannies of her petty princes has called Italy into the possession and manifest enjoyment of new life. In Florence, in Rome. in Naples, in answer to our inquiries whether the advent of Victor Emmanuel had not been attended with a great increase of peace, security to life and property, and consequent prosperity, the same glad response in the affirmative was received, and the evidences were everywhere visible. Would that her religious life were as satisfactory as her political life is now progTessive and promising. We were greatly pleased with a conversa- tion we had with a thoughtful and large-hearted Italian gentleman on our way across the Mediterranean. Admitting all the political advantages they now, as a nation, enjoy, he said. "Our people want religion and they can never rise into true greatness without it. They call themselves free- thinkere,' but the truth is they do not think at all. In the rebound from priestly domination, their hatred of all religion is wild and unreasoning in the extreme. What nay country will require, and should have, is the Christianity of the New Testament presented in its simplest original forms, introduced by plain Scripturally enlightened men, without the aid or intervention of any clerical caste whatever. Small communities should be formed, in which believers would come together to search the scriptures and edify one another in a scriptural way. " I am sure," said he, "the 'Ault would be glorious." The above is the substance of our long and interesting conversa- tion. As we travelled towards Rome, along the valley of die Tiber, the absence of either village, town, or city, except those which stood on the very summits of the hills, spoke to us powerfully of the ages of bloodshed and rapine that had rolled over the Roman Empire, and, in later years, of the Roman states, during which these fortified cities had been held, sometimes fir the defence, but more frequently for the crushing out of human IMerty, ever guarding the imperial city from attack like a b:rlt of iron or a wall of fire. Looking out from one window of the carriage might have been seen one of the old fortresses frowning down upon os, while from the other could be seen in beautiful contrast a couple of women, distaff in hand, watching over their few sheep, the very emblem of peace and contented industry, and surely an earnest of the time when men shall " beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning - hooks."

ROME. Eager was the outlook of our party as we drew near to Rome, and a cheer of gladness broke from us as the mighty dome of St. Peter's stood out against the evening sky. It was a thrilling moment to find ourselves near the great city whose supeestition and iron dominion had formed so great a part of the history of the world. But all such feelings speedily vanished as we found ourselves face to face with the din and uproar of the railway square. Such pulling, hauling, screaming, and shouting I never experienced. Thankful, indeed, were we when we found ourselves com- fortably domiciled in the Hotel Angelo American. Our first impulse, after dinner, was to rush off to St. Peter's. After traversing one or two good streets we came to the bridge of St. Angelo, with its ten angels standing on the parapet. These dignities, being evidently of a Roman type, wings notwithstanding, we did not honour with much of our atten- tion, but pressing rapidly on, soon found ourselves in the long narrow footpaths, with the heavy stone houses tower- above Ls, and two or three feet above the line of vision, strong iron bars project in a bend from the first storey win- dow-sills as far as the eye can reach, telling a sad tale of insecurity in the long ages of tyranny just departed. We must have travelled a mile or more before we had St. Peter's towering in front of us, in the great Piazza bearing its name. Dark as it was we could not see much of it, nor of its sur- roundings; but we thought, as we came hack, and glanced up the dismal lanes and alleys, and had our footsteps dog- ged by importunate and ill looking beggars, that it was rather a mistake to venture on such a path at night time. Probably during Pio Nono's reign it might have been worse for us than we found it. We had other opportunities of see- ing St. Peter's, but how shou'd I attempt to dwell on its "glorious beauty," after it has been described by travellers and guide books without nursber. Let it Suffice to give a specimen of how both speak of it. CharlC3 Dickens, describing its external surroundings says," The beauty of the Piazza in which it stands, with its clusters of exquisite columns, and its gush- ing fountains, so fresh, so broad, and free, and beautiful —nothing can exaggerate." Now, were I to say that the fountains, with their clouds of spray glistening in the sun- shine, are even more beautiful than he has described, but that the columns impressed me neither with their immensity nor magnificence, and that it seemed to me an amazing and unmeaning waste of money to raise four rows of lofty columns close to each other without any edifice above or behind for them to support or adorn, I tear I should be re- garded as presumptuous. And, surely, it is a vain thing to talk of gextravagant expenditure, with the fact before us that the church, when completed, cost £12,000,000 sterling, at a time when money was three times the value it is now. Describing, the interior, the guidebook qnotes from Eustace in the following elevated strain : " Enter ! its grandeur overwhelms thee not!" " The most extensive hall ever constructed by human art expands in magnificent perspective before you. Advancing up the nave you admire the beauty of the variegated marble under your feet, and the splendour of the golden vault overhead, the lefty Corinthian pilasters with their bold emablature, the intermediate niches with their statues, the arcades with the graceful figures that recline on the curves of the arches. When you reach the foot of the altar, and ,standing in the centre of the church, contemplate the four superb vistas that open around you, and then raise your eyes to the dome, at the prodigious elevation of 400 feet, extending like a firmament over your head, and presenting, in glowing mosaic, the companies of the just, and the choirs of celestial spirits, &c." After that, who dare lift a little finger of qualifying praise, or presume to speak, as I do in my note-book, of "the chaster beauty of St. Paolo, so ex- quisite in its proportions, se elevated in its style, so chaste and consistent in its matchless details." And yet I feel confident that a comparison of the photographs in my , possession would give the palm to St. Yaolo in these respects. I But it is quite certain that no description can give an adequate idea of the treasures of art and wonders, of archi- tectural skill which have been laid under contribution to adorn and beautify these gorgeous piles, and to enrich, besides, the world-renowned galleries of the Vatican. I can- not help saying a word or two about the celebrated bronze statue of "St. Peter." The figure, not in the least remark- able for beauty, is sitting under a canopy of crimson and gold, out of all keeping with the exquisite ornamentation of the place. One foot projects a little beyond the other, and over the edge of the slab on which the figure site. From the point of the big toe and the one next to it a good part of an inch has disappeared, kissed away, they have the audacity to say. The Castle of Angelo, in the very centre of the city, and on the edge of the. Tiber, is well-deserving of notice on its own account as a massive and magnificent fortress; but I mention it in order to emphasize the fact, that the remains of Hadrian, the Roman Emperor, whose , vigorous reign has left lie impressive marks upon every part I of the world over which the wings of the Roman eagle 1 anciently flew, wete buried here, with those of all his imme- diate successors down to the beginning of the third century; and that his porphyry sarcophagus, removed hence, is now used as a font in one of the chapels of St. Peter's. As an illustration of the ignoble ends to which the most magni- ficent of human works may descend, the theatre of slarcellus stands out pre-eminent. Planned by Julius Ctesar, built by his son Caesar Augustus, and transferred by him to his son-in-law Marcellus, its outer walls now form I the corner of two streets in one of the lowest and dirtiest parts of Rome. The building is still grand in its utter degradation. The lower storey is in the simple Doric, the seccnd in the moretraceful lonic, and the third in the still more ornate Corinthian order. Bold would be the attempt lo penetrate into the mvsteriee of the upper storeys; the basement, however, cannot be hid. There the blacksmith blows his fire, and wields his hammer in the sight of all , men ; the coal vender wheels his barrow in. and out of another door, and the greengrocer parades his cabba of ges and potatoes in a third. So much for the dreams Julius Omar and Cesar Augustus, of whom it is written that he shrunk from the honour of appropriating to himself so great a work, and therefore shared it with his beloved son-in-law. Little do the barbarians in possession know or dream of the aspirations of its imperial founders, or that twenty centuries tower, with their wonderful cycles, above their uncombed heads. Perhaps more unconscious than even these men of the faded glories by which she was surrounded sat a quiet woman, knitting a stocking, at an open window, within a yard' or two of the "Portico di Octavia." This great work was dedicated to Octavio by her brother Augustus, and, as the description on the architrave states, was restored by Septimus Severus and Caracalla. This poor woman, thought I, knows probably nothing be- yond the fact that she is sitting near to an old arch, and cares nothing beyond finishing her stocking at a certain time. The circular temple of -H .rcules with its 20 beauli- ful Corinthian columns, built AD. 75, Pleased us much. A I very interesting object close to it is the arch of Janus—a ' massive double arch, supposed to be the entrance of the ancient cattle market and its neighbouring traffic. Within a stone's throw of this is the house of "Rienzie, the last of the Tribunes." Then we go down a narrow road opposite, and making a turn, descend to the celebrated "Cloaca Maxima," or great drain, made 530 years before Christ, and still performing service as a sewer to Rome. As a relic of antiquity it was more iateresting than enjeyable; tile stench, owing to a rise in the Tiber, making us glad to retreat. As we passed up the archway we saw nine women stooping OVer a running underground stream washing clothes; and! such washing I It would have sent a thrifty housekeeper into fits to see them dashing the linen against the stones, and rubbing end scrubbing them as if for their lives. The Uolosseuml so often described, but so seldom grasped in thought, or retained on the nage of memory when once beheld. How shall I give even a faint conception of its magnitude, or the grandeur of ite proportions? The poet Must 008 to to my aid t

div.head: TIIESDAY.—Before Alderman Webster.
div.p: TIIESDAY.—Before Alderman Webster.

A DESERTER.—Henry Jones, a young man, was charged with being a deserter from Her Majesty's 55th Regiment of Foot, stationed at Shorncliffe.—P. C. Jones said he was on duty in the police office when the prisaner came in, and asked for a ticket for admission to the workhouse. He asked prisoner if he bad been in the army, but he denied baying been in, although he said he had been in the militia. Witness then examined the prisoner's boots, and found they were military boots, and on charging the prisoner with desertion, he admitted the offence. Remanded for safe custody. THIIRSDA 2. —Before Captain Litton, Captain Reynolds, and Ziba Armitage, Esq. THEFT FROM AN UNCLE—Bridget McDonough,a young woman, was charged with stealing from the house of John McDonough, Glass House-row, a silver geneva watch, value £l, and a white shirt front, and two pocket handkerchiefs. Prisoner pleaded guilty.—From the evidence of the Chief- Constable, it appeared that the prisoner's uncle Hugh, living at Bold, occasionally came to Warrington, where he lodged with his brother. On the 13th instant he paid a visit and placed a watch and some articles of clothing in a box which was placed in prisoner's room. Some time after- wards the articles were missed, and subsequently found to have been pawned by the prisoner.—This was prisoner's fourth appearance, and she was sent to gaol for three months. Cunt FOR COMPENSATION.—James White was Sam- moned by Captain Reynolds for neglecting to fulfill hia contract, ss. being claimed as coropensation.—Captain Rey- nolds said there was a written rule in his works that the master should give a week's notice, and the men likewise. The defendant left without notice, putting complainant to some inconvenience and loss. fla had not asked for a week's wages, and the money claimed would be put into the Hospital box.—An order was made for the amount. AT TACK UPON A WOMAN WITH A CLoo.—Catherine and Mary Connolly, sisters, were charged with assaulting Eliza- beth Tunstall, on Saturday night. Mary sent a girl to borrow a comb from the complainant, who, however, would not lend it, and Catherine went and dragged complainant from her own house by the hair of the head. Mary then came on the scene and between them they dragged com- plainant to defendants' door, where Catherine pulled off her clog with which she struck her on the head. Complainant was in such a state after this usage that she had to be car- ried home.—The defendants seemed in great trouble, and said they had their dead father in the house.—Complainant said she did not wish to press the case, and the Bench under the circumstances erdered the defendants to pay the costs. CONJVCIAL Irtrxmcrry.—lionour Barnes and John Butler, brother and sister, were charged with assaulting Mary Butler, on Saturday ni2ht.—Complainant stated that about six o'clock, when she was in the street, Barnes got hold of her by the hair and pulled her to the ground, then struck her savagely on the face. The crowd whieh had collected released her, and she was on her way home, when Butler, who is her husband, met her, end struck her a blow on the nose, which bled freely.—Defendant Butler made a long statement as to his wife's actions, but the Bench said there was no doubt he had ill-used his wife, and be would be fined 20s. and I.os. costs. Barnes was fined 55. and costs. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—Richard Looker was summoned by Robert Tickle for using language calculated to provoke a breach of the peace, and he was bound over to keep the peace for six months. _

RUNCORNIANS INTERVIEWING MR. JOHN BRIGHT. Mr. Cooke, the managing secretary of the Young Men's Christian Association at Runcorn, formed one of a deputa- tion from that district to the 26th annual sermon of the National Division of the Sons of Temperance, keld at-Run- corn. He has given our representative an account of an interview which the deputation had with the renowned orator. Mr. John Bright, which may be summarised as follows: —" From the park we strolled towards 'One Ash' and we were suddenly struck witb the idea of- calling to see Mr. Brigbt. It seemed an almost unwarrantable intrusion,; but the desire to see the great tribune of the-people became over- mastering, and WC marched up the front and asked for him. We were well received by the servant, who informed us her master was out, but would be in soon—in about an hour. She seemed anxious that we should see him. We walked on towards a farm on the further heights—a quaint old place, beautifully situated on a rising ground, commanding a splendid: view of fine scenery for tmles round. We got in conversation, with the mistress, whose parents, it turned out, were natives of Runcorn. It must have been a long time ago when they lived here, for she was eighty years of age, and had been on that farm for fifty-seven years. However, ' she was pleased to meet with people hailing from Runcorn, and regaled us with oat-cake and,milk. She was delighted l to tell us that she had supplied the Bright family with milk for over fifty years, and spoke of the kindness the members of the family had shown. 'Mr. John,' as she called him, woukl often stroll up to the farm and have a chat: he wae.a nice plain gentleman.' We were all the more wishful to have an interview with Mr. Bright after what we had heard from the old lady; and after bidding her good-bye, we retraced our steps to ' One Ash. We were just in time to meet him returning from his even- walk, Finding ourselves so suddenly in the presence of the ' great orator and statesmen we were somewhat confused; but he soon made us feel at home by his kindly manner. When we told him who we were, and that we, were conneated with the Sons of Teirraerance, and called, to his remembrance some passages from his speeches on the Irish Sunday Clos- ing Bill, he got fairly into swing, and gave somemost telling remarks on the social aspect of the question we have so much at heart. Re said drink was a curse. He knew of families in that neighbourhood who had suffered great dis- aster from its use, and though it had killed several membhrs of those families, they would not banish it from their houses —they would still put the devil on the table. They would not think of acting in such a manner with small-pox, scarlet fever, or any of those evils; but would jealously guard their homes against their approach. He could not understand how people could be so foolish. They would see a very different state of things if people would but give up drink, seeing the amount of pauperism and crime resulting from it. It was now about half' past nine, and the hon. gentleman shook hands with tie, and wishea us good night. We plucked a flower from the garden as a souvenir of our visit. I think our visit to Rochdale was equal to any trip we might have been induced to take had we remained in Runcorn durisz , the Whitsuntide holidsys.".
POWASEM

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 18, 1881. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting took place on Tuesday afternoon,l at the Board-room, Alforde Chambers. Major Cross pre-, sided, and there were also present—Messrs. Shuttleworth Handley, Kershaw, Knight, Gossage, O'Keeffe, Gaskell, jun., Heve.. Pankhurst, Br9wr., Carey, Heasley (law clerk), _ , , • A Mai Oppenheirti (clerk pro tem.,, (acectunOpt), Roberta (engineer), and Higginsc: 'surveyor). TWO I SIONATIONS. The CHAIRMAN said he Lad received a communication from Mr. Carlile (Messrs. J. W. Carlile and Co., contractors, dtc,) stating that owing to his "difficulties," he was sorry to announce his intention of resigning his seat on the Board. After the many years he had had the honour of being con- nected with the members it was extremely painful to him to have to put before them his resignation; but under the present circumstances there was no other course open to him. In conclusion, he asked Major Cross and the mem- bers to accept his best thanks for the courtesy and kindness he had always received at their hands. The speaker said he had to submit to them a resolution containing a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Carlile for the services he had rendered the Board in the past, and expressing their regret that they would be deprived of his valuable help in the future.—The resolution was passed nem dos—The CHAIRMAN next moved that the resignation of Mr. Wells, the consideration of which had been postponed until that morning, be accepted, and that a similar resolution to that ordered to be sent to Mr. Carlile be forwarded to him.— The resolution was carried unanimously.—Mr. GosseoN moved that Mr. David Foster be elected to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. Wells.—Mr. CAREY se- conded the motion.—Mr. KERSHAW proposed that Mr. John Houghton be elected, but the motion was not seconded.— Mr. BROWN had pleasure in proposing that Mr. Samuel Sadler be appointed to the position, and argued that he was certainly entitled to the suffrages of the members owing to having occupied the next place, in point of numbers, to the last of the successful candidates at the annual election.—Mr. PANICHURST seconded the resolution.—At this point some discussion took place as to the eligibility of Mr. Wells for re-election, Dr. O'Keeffe having proposed it. A general opinion was expressed that it would not be possible for Mr. Wells to accept the position, owing to his living out of the district; and the mover said he would withdraw his resolu- tion.—Six members voted for the amendment in favour of the vacancy being given to Mr. Samuel Sadler, and five against, on which the Chairman declared it carried; and it was afterwards passed as a substantive motion.—Mr. Gos- SAGE then proposed that Mr. David Foster be elected in place of Mr. Carlile, and the proposition was carried unanimously. THE TOUR OS' INSPECTION. After a brief discussion it was decided that it would be well that the customary animal tour for the inspection of the works belonging to the Board should be made. On the motion of Mr. BROWN, seconded by Mr. Kumla, the date of the tour was fixed for the sth 'July. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. Mr. GASICELL moved the adoption of the minutes of this committee, and Mr. BROWN seconded the motion, which was carried. They stated that the total quantity of water de- livered during the four weeks ending May 25th had been 40,483,200 gallons, compared with 41,036,671 gallons for the previous year, or a decrease of 1-34 per cent. The quantity in stock on the 25th May was 10,800,697 gallons. There had been a decrease of 351,000 cubic feet in the gas made during the four weeks above named, or 8-25 per cent., and adecrease of 303,000 cubic feet, or 6.99 per cent, in the quantity sent out, as compared with the corresponding period last year. The tender of Messrs. Smethurst, Hoyle, and Grime, for the supply of gas coal for three years, sub- ject to the price for the first year being Bs. 6d. per ton, for the second 9s. per ton, and for the third year 9e. 6d. per ton, was accepted. The price of coke had been raised to Bs. per ton.

div.head: HIGENCLY COMMITTEE.
div.p: HIGENCLY COMMITTEE.

From these minutes it appeared that the committee re- commended the foot walk in front of the Catholic church in Lugsdale-road be flagged, at an estimated cost of £3O. The surveyor had been instructed to proceed without delay with the completion of the widening of Victoria and Widnes roads, in accordance with the Board's agreement with the Leigh estate. An interview had taken place with Mr. All- card on behalf of the Runcorn Property and Investment Com- pany, as to the widening of Lower House-lane, and it was recommended that the footpath should be made nine feet wide, and the Board should set back the fence and make a cindered footpath. Resolved, that the Law Clerk be in- structed to write to the London and North-Western Rail- way Company, calling their attention to the dangerous springing back of the large gates at Waterloo-road when being opened,"and to request that the company will cause a number, to distinguish the men on duty, to be placed out- side the signal-box at each of the crossings. Mr. Allcard had submitted a plan as to the proposed improvement of the public highway at Whitfield's Cross. Crow Wood, op- posite property belonging o the trustees of the Tate Mr. J. Spinks; and it had been resolved that in consideration of the land shown on the plan being added to the highway, the Board be recommended to kerb and form a foot walk of blue bricks co-extensive with the land given up, when the build ings are erected. The surveyor was instructed to renew the fingetposts in the district, where requisite, and to restore the remainder.—The minutes were approved, on the proposition of Mr. KERSHAW, seconded by Mr. Platstegualsr.—lt was stated that it had been decided not to proceed with the pro- posal as to paving at the front of Warrington-road Board schools. MILTON CHAPEL CONGREGATIONALISTS AND THE BOARD. Mr. CARET referred to the proposal to pay a sum to the Milton Congregational Church, on condition that they gave up a certain amount of land to the Board. He asked whether it would not be possible to postpone the m itter for the present, and whether the payment had been taken into account in making out the estimate of the committee for the coming year.—Mr. KERSHAW said the Board had offered to pay the church £175 for the land, but, considering the amount which had been paid in the case of the Wesleyan Methodist Chapel under somewhat similar circumstances, they considered the sum too small.—A deputation consist- ing of the Rev. T. Peters, pastor of the church, Mr. Rimmer and Mr. W. Findlow' were then introduced to the Beard.— After a few remarks from the Chairman Mr. PETERS said it appeared to him that the last offer made by the church to the Board, would have to be either accepted or rejected.—A brief discussion followed, and the deputation then left the room. They were shortly afterwards called in again, and the Chairman said the membershad decided that they would ! not undertake to ',mild the boundary wall themselves, but would make the church an offer of £2OO, to be paid to them after they had put up a substantial boundary wall. They would give the church until the next meeting of the com- mittee, to either reject or accept the offer.—The Rev. T. PETERS intimated that. the church did not consider the pro- posal sufficiently liberal, after which the deputation left.— Shortly Velar° the termination of the meeting, a letter was handed in from the deputation, stating that they would accept the olio of the Board on consideration that they would say guineas instead of pounds in their offer.—The CHAIRMAN said that the Board could not make any altera- tion in their proposal.

div.head: KIALTH COMEfrITEE.
div.p: KIALTH COMEfrITEE.

The minutes were approved, on the motion of Mr. CAREY, I seconded by Mr. HANDLEY. They contained the medical I officer's report, which showed that the births during the last month had been 97. or 46.5 per 1,000, and the death 26, or 12'8 per 1,000, including 10 of children under one year, and five of children between one and five yea's. There had been one death from zymotic disease, and three inquests. The Nuisance Inspector (Mr. Dickson) reported the action which had.been taken in reference to the outfall sewer me West Bank, under the direction of Mr. Carey. Mr. Glover had repeated his promise to remedy the nuisanc3 at Whit- suntide. There had been one fatal case of scarlet fever; two cases-of typhoid, and, at a hoarse in Mill Brow, two cases of measles had occnrred, but the patients were recovering. The surveyor was instructed to have in readiness for the next Beard meeting the plans for the drainage of Halton View, nose Bank, Albert-road, Lugsdale-lane, Warrington- road, and Lugsdale-road, which had been approved by the committee.

FINANCE.—THS 7AsTnIATEs. From the finance minutes, it appeared that it was recom- mended that the Board, on the application of Mr. R. Shaw, remit the plying expenses, amounting to £6l, apportioned to the-United Methodist Free Church, Oakland-street, in RC- cordance with section 151 of the Public Health Act, 1875. Resolved that the estimates of theseveral committees for the current year be. recommended for adoption, and that a, General District Rate of 2s. 0d.., in the £ on buildings, and 714 on land, he laid. Tenders were presented from Mr. T. S. S,'wsle, and Mr. A. Edwards, for printing of the Board's minutes and mobthly summonses to the members, and that otMr. Edwards at ls. 6d. per Page, being the lowest,.was areeepted.—Mr. HAYES moved the adoption of the minutes and the passing of the rate. He stated that.the estimates of the various committees fOr the expenditure• of next year • were as follows :—Highway, £4,668 1054 health, .£1,197 10s; market, £9d; hospital, am 165.; and finance,4,lBo. Mr. GASICELL seconded the resolution, and expressed a hope ' that in the present state of Widnes the committees would do their best to keep strictly within the lines cf their esti- mates.

Mr. GOSSAGE, J.P., explained that the looal Bench were agreeable to let the police court room for the purpose of being used as a comity court, ou payment being made for cleaning and other incidental expenses. The Board resolved that the signature of the chairman should be affixed to the pethion which has been got up. by Mr. Husband, solicitor, assisted by several other gentlemen, setting forth the urgent necessity which exists for the town: being granted local county court privileges equal to several of its neighbours. THE LAW CLEWS'S BILL OF COSTS.

A comtnunication was read by the Chairman from Mr. Darlington, the Local Government Board auditor, stating that he could not undertake the work of auditing the bill for law costs presented by Mr. Beasley, and the proper course for the Board to adopt wouldte to submit it to the Clerk of the Peace at Preston.—The meeting agreed that the docu- ment should be sent on to the Clerk of the Peace. TEE SEWERAGE SCHEME.

Mr. liroorNosobr—, surveyor, submitted a scheme for sewer- jog the district at acost of p 2,900, as against the one pro- posed by the committee, which it was said at the time would cost £38,000. At the request ef Mr. Kershaw, he under- took to elplain the matter to the Board.
