div.head: REVISED VE[iSION,
div.p: THE REVISED VE[iSION,

LECTURE Jfi' MR. BEET, AT RUNCORN. On Thum:lay evening the Rev. J. A. Beet, of Warrington, delivered a lecture in Bethesda Congregational school-room, Runcorn, under P. 19 napicea of the Young Men's Christian
Association, on "The Revised New Testament." Mr. Lyon
There was A poor attendance. The proceedings were commenced by the singing of "Before Jehovah's awful
throne," and prayer by Mr. C. Garnett.
The CHAIRMAN, in introducing the lecturOt/ fiterts4 the importance of the work of revising the New Testament, whether they reviewed the matter as affecting the various
religious denominations, or in its influence and effects upon the Christianity of the country. Having spoken upon the feel- ing which the suggestion to revise the New Testament . . . . .

• . --- caused at the time when it was proposed to go on with the work, he remarked that, personally, he felt some regret that the revisers had found it necessary to make changes in the Lord's Prayer. Let them, for instance take the phrase "Deliver us from evil," now rendered, "Deliver us from the evil one." It seemed to him that the expression in the authorised version was far more comprehensive. In conclusion, Mr. Lyon spoke of the peaceful manner in which Ithe present revisers had pursued their work in the Jerusalem
Chaamber,_as compared with the dangers_ which the first
revisers Of the Bible had to meet. iiet then bii-eflTintro- duced Mr. Beet to the meeting.

The LECTURER first expressed his pleasure at meeting his old friends in Runcorn once more. He somewhat regretted that he had allowed the few remarks which he intended to make that night to be dignified by the name of a lecture, as he never "lectured." He should simply try to give them some idea of the process by which the revision had been made. Having spoken of the conception which we, as human beings, naturally formed of how we should have proceeded in case we had been giving to the world such a book as the New Testament, he dwelt briefly upon the foreknowledge of God, and His apparent decision to leave His word to the risks of literary composition. The difference between St. Paul's language and our own was very much greater than the French language as compared with the English. The same thoughts floated in the French as in the English lan- guages, but it was not so in the ancient Greek tongue. The whole of the New Testament was probably written in Greek. The copying of the various documents opened up fl way to errors manifold, whereas printing did not. Having explained the difference between the term " read- ing" and "rendering," he commended to the audience the " Variorum Bible" lately published. The lecturer first spoke of textual criticism, and referred to the various . . . . . .

ancient copies of the Scriptures. Speaking of the Alexan- drian copy, he said it was kept in the British Museum, under a glass case, and was one of the oldest manuscripts of the Scriptures in the world. The age of it wis about 1,400 years and it was presented to King Charles the First by the Patriarch of Constantinople. The pages of this book were written upon calf skin, and there was no division between the words, so that the manuscript was very diffi- cult to decipher. A good many of the words were con- tracted, others mis-spelled, and some altered. It seemed generally agreed that the best of the manuscripts was the one to be found in the Vatican library at Rome, which heat one time had had the pleasure of inspecting whilst on a visit to the eternal city. Mr. Beet then gave a brief . .

account of the visit of the great scholar Tischendorf to the monastery where he discovered the Sinaitic manuscript of the Scriptures. He thought it ought to be known that the late Emperor of Russia was a great friend of Tischendorf, and it was really through the Emperor's assistance that the manuscript was recovered. It was chiefly in the three languages in which the words about Christ were written on the cross, that the story of the Saviour had come , down to us. He was glad to say that the Alexandrian manuscript had now been photographed, and so beautifully ' bad the work been done, that the very grain of the parch- ment was quite clear. He was pleased to state that the new version was altogether honest—there was nothing kept back. In every case the word had been used in favour of which the evidence preponderated. Where there was a doubt the revisers had put the word into the margin and in nearly every case where they found nothing in the margin, they might accept what was given as nearly practically certain. In the new version there were a few texts omitted which were formerly thed to support the divinity of our Lord , Jesus Christ. The passage in the epistle of John about the I three witnesses, was omitted. He might give them in- stances of passages which had been so rendered as to I strengthen the proofs as to the divinity of Christ. There I was one passage in the new version—" Sanctify the Lord 1 Christ in your hearts "—which certainly could only refer to something that pertained to God only. Then there was another "No man bath seen God at any time; the only be- gotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, He bath declared him." Textual criticism and the revised version showed that the passage ought to read "He who is God only begotten which is in the bosom of the Father." Tischendorf's manuscript went a great way to settle this matter. He felt very strongly that the new version was a vast gain. He used to read in Revelations about four beasts which were before the throne; and he was glad that they were gone,—(laughter)—for now they were represented by "four living creatures." It would be remembered that these "living creatures" were spoken of in the book of Ezekiel, and as the passage bad now been rendered it connected the two mysterious books of the Bible —Revelations and Ezekiel—in a very interesting manner. There was the passage in the authorised version which read "The flesh lusteth against the Spirit * * * so that ye cannot do the things that ye would." He had heard that passage quoted as if it were impossible for us to do the good things which we would ; but the revised version threw a great light upon it, giving it as or "ye may not do the things that ye would." That itself was a very great gain. On looking back, he believed he was the first who advocated revision in a Methodist publication. In conclusion the lecturer re- ferred to the many advances in science which had been made durirp, the nineteenth century, and he thought that the age had been fl•tingly crowned by the sublime work 0 the revision of the Bible. (Loud applause.) Mr. TIMOTIIY SECS ME, in moving a vote of thanks to the Lecturer, said be looked upon the revised version as a great gain to preachers and Sabbath school teachers. He referred to the high position which the " Commentary on the Romans," written by Mr. Beet, had taken in the country, and expressed himself very pleased to see his old friend. Mr. MATISITALL seconded the resolution, which was paused with applause. A similar compliment was paid to Mr. Lyon, on the pro- position of Mr. BEET, seconded by Mr. GARNETT, and the proceeings terminated the singing of the Doxolcey.

div.head: RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.

The-aonual meeting was held on Wednesday evening, at the Board-room, Town Hall, for the purpose of electing a chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. George Marshall pre- sided, and there were aloe present Messrs. Steele, Norman, Lyon, McDougall, Doboon, Williams, J. J. Speakman, P. Speakman, Hazlehurst, Taylor. Handley, Shaw, Moadow- croft, Linaker, (clerk), Brookes (secretary), and Barker (surveyor).

STELE, on taking his position as chairman, thanked the I members for the confidence they had shown in him by electing him their chairman. Certainly the position was onE .0i soma difficulty, but he would do his beat to discharge his duties to their sat!sfaction.—This concluded the business of the annual meeting, and that of the adjourned meg* 'fleeting was then proceeded with,

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF CILAIRMAN.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF CILAIRMAN.

The CHAIRMAN, before proceeding to the ordinary busi- ness,,first referred to the honour which he had felt it to be to preside ever such an assembly of gentlemen during the pact year. He reviewed the work of the Board daring the twelvemonths, and congratulated the members on obtaining so great a boon as a concession as to water supply on con- ditlen of their withdrawing the opposition to the Liverpool Corporation Water Bill. The possession of a good supply of water by the town must have a strong tendency to promote the development of Manufacturing in their midst. He was glad to know that the hospital question was in so fair a way of being settled to the satisfaction of the ratepayers, and that otherwise, useful and economical improvements hod been carried out during his term of office. He regretted the dulness of trade, the severe winter, and hoped that they would shortly sea a revival of commercial prosperity. He was also sorry that the Board had not been able to obtain the requisite coneession from the i\larquis of Chohnondeley in the matter of' the heath, which, if granted, would have enabled them to have secureda public park for the benefit of the people. He thanked all the Commissioners who by their kindness,and support had helped him in the duties which devolved upon the chairman. He trusted that he re- tired from the position with all their good wishes. He could, at any rate, say that they all had his best wishes; and he hoped that under the gentlemeh. who would during the coming year preside over their delibera- tions, Rtnicorn would continua to gourish. Dr. McDonoma, then rose to propose that Dr. Steele should be chairman of the Board during the ensuing year. He fait sure that-the gentleman in question would discharge his duties with satisfaction to himself and advantage to the public;: that he would maintain the best traditions of the Board, and preserve to its members the liberty of free speech —its most precious, inheritance. He hoped that at the end of tho year Dr. Steele would be able to say that it had been both a happy and: prosperous one.—Mr. Donsox was of opinion that the ability which Dr. Steele had disphyed, and the gentlemanly manner in which he had at all times con- ducted himself whilst he bad.been a member of the Board, proved that he was in every way worthy of being appointed to so distinguished a position.. He had no doubt thp.t if Dr. Steele was elected he wouU make it a careful, study to dis- charge his duties efficiently.—The motion was carried unani- mously.—Previous to De Steele taking the choir, Mr. HANDLE! said he thougbt it would be most ungracious on the part of the members if they didnot express to Mr. Mar- shall their sense of the services he had rendered whilst he had been chairman. Mr. Marshall had, had many difficult duties to perform during the twelvemonths; and though all had not beenlmooth sailing daring that time, he considered that he had conducted the business with a fair amount of credit to the Board. On retiring from the position, their late chairman would have the pleasure of feeling that he had done some little to add to the prosperity of Rumba.— Mr. NORMAN seconded the resolution, which was carried unanimously.—Mr. MARSHALL, in responding, expressed the pleasure it afforded him to know that he bad performed his luties to the satisfaction of the members. He had done his best, and if he had fallen short, it had not arisen from the want of will, but from the lack of ability., He hoped that under their new chairman they might ital continue to work for the general benedt of the town and the ratepayers,l)r.

THE DETERMINED SUICIDE AT WARRINGTON. Mr. C. E. Drifileld, county, coroner, held an inqeeet at the Black Horse Inn, Sankey' Bridget!, on. Tuesday, on the body of Thomas Alexander Livingstone, :who committed suicide in a determined manner ron Saturday, The particulars of the case were fully reported in the second edition of The Examiner on Saturday. The first witness called was Gee. Henry Wood, 16 years of age, living at 106, Plerpoint-street, Warrington, and employed as a "picker-up" at the forge. He said that on Saturday, about 12-25, he was going away from Mr. Warburton's, when he saw the deceased walk into the canal, from the Sankey Bridges side, "right to the middle," wheri he held up his hands and sank in the water. lie came up again, and bubbles came from his mouth. He sank again, and witness thought of pulling off his clothes and jumping in after him, but a man who was there told him not to do so, "as the water was poisonous." Witness then ran to Sankey and informed the police of the occur- , renze. Deceased never spoke whilst in the water. Deceased had the whole of his clothes on.—Edward Lewis, gardener, Bewsey Old Hall, Burtottwood, said a boy went to his house about 12-30 on Saturday, and told him that there was a man drowning himself in the canal. He went en the turn bridge, and seeing deceased at the surface, be sent his wife for a clothes prop. With this he tried to reach the drowning man, bat it was too short, and intelli- gence was sent to the Lockhouse. When the men were coming from this place deceased sank, and did I not again come to- the surface. Deceased made no attempt I to save himself. With the aid of the loekrake the body was I recovered in about 20 minutes time. There were no wounds on the body.—Cidilia Livingstone, living at 55, Orford-lane, Warrington, said the deceased was her husband, and was about 65 years of age. He had been in the army many years, but had lately assisted his son Alexander, who is a foreman for Mr. Collins, builder. On Saturday deceased rose early; as was his usual practice, and complained of his head. She wished him to stay in bed but he would not, and I after dressing himself, she heard him go out. He did not I return during the day, and in the evening the police officer brought her word of his death in the canal. Deceased's son I had not seen him either. For the last six months deceased I hal been in a desponding state of mind. He had a trouble previously which took great hold of his mind. Twice he had mentioned to her that he should come to an untimely end, which frightened her so much that she put the razors and knives out of his way, and when he was at home she took care to be ,with him. They had had.-no quarrel, and and abe knew nothing in the matter but what she had mentioned. Deceasedre father hanged himself, and his only sister died in an asylum. She remembered some tine ago buying some flannel to make him some clothing, and when she told him he said," You may have it yourself; I don't think I shall ever wear it." He never changed from his despondency, but would sit ia the house without speak- ing to- auyone. Deceased had no reason to go to Sankey Bridges, as he had no friends or work to de there. He had worked 21 years for Mr. Bolton.—By the Foreman: He had worked at Sankey Chapel and might be going there. Deceased did not take much-drink.—The Coroner, in slim- ming up, said it was evident the man went to the canal with the intention of committing suicide, and this view was sup- ported by the facts that he had previously threatened him- self, and that his wife had hidden razors and knives from -him. And when they found that two members of the family badheed insane—one causing his cloth and the other dying in an asylum--he thought they need not go far for an ex- planation of the matter, or hesitate to say that the act was committed whilst the- man was temporarily insane. A ver- dict to the effect that deceased committed suicide whilst of unsound mind was returned:

div.p: BAPTIST CHURCHES.

The annual meoting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Association of Baptist Churches was opened at Ashton- under-Lyne on Wednesday, Mr. E. Mounsey, of Liverpool, moderator, presiding. There was a very numerous atten- dance of ministers and delegates from the various churches in the two counties.

The MODERATOR, in his opening remarks, stated that since 1870 the churches connected with the association had increased from 54 to 1014 and the membership had about doubled. While this had been done in shout 10 years, it took about 27 of the previous years to double the rnembei- ship, while the churches increased by only 17. Referring to arkeffort which was being made to increase the rass.cia- tion mission fund, he said lie did not think they ought to be so far behind their Congregational brethren as they were. The Rev.
